utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: lean sale outreach period to additional resources early on in the process, such as HPD's homeowner help desk.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: And increasing water and sewer debt enforcement threshold for inclusion in the at-risk pool, we are raising the threshold for eligible Class 1, 2, and 3 family homes from $3,000

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: to $5,000 of debt older than one year.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: Single-family homes remain exempt.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: Deputy Commissioner Hill can provide additional details about the changes in the lien sale if you would like to hear further.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Yeah, that would be great, Deputy Commissioner.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Good to see you.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: I do want to acknowledge that it was our council who authorized or who is allowing the administration to pursue a lien sale in 2027.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: We implemented many reforms.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: They were very thoughtful.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: I want to highlight Councilmember Sandy Nurse for her work and the work of the Tax Lien, Abolish the Tax Lien Sale Coalition for all of their recommendations.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: I think specifically it would be helpful to hear you talk about the ways in which your plans for 2027 comply with the city council's laws in addition to some of the protections that First Deputy Commissioner has mentioned.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: I'm sorry, but before anything, will you raise your right hand?

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Do you affirm to tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth before these committees?

utterances.speaker: Annette Hill
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: You may proceed.

chapters.summary: Annette Hill, DOF Deputy Commissioner, details plans to share at-risk list with nonprofits earlier, expand data sharing for text/email notifications, add deed theft info to notices, and expand payment options and Easy Exit program.
chapters.title: Deputy Commissioner Hill outlines 2027 lien sale outreach and payment reforms

utterances.speaker: Annette Hill
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Annette Hill
utterances.text: I have to apologize.

utterances.speaker: Annette Hill
utterances.text: I have a cold.

utterances.speaker: Annette Hill
utterances.text: I'm not going to sound very well, but I'll try my best.

utterances.speaker: Annette Hill
utterances.text: And thank you, members of the committee.

utterances.speaker: Annette Hill
utterances.text: The city will strengthen outreach and notification process to ensure homeowners are aware of their debts and the opportunities for resolution before the lien sale by

utterances.speaker: Annette Hill
utterances.text: sharing the at-risk list with nonprofit partners earlier than the 90-day launch to allow for additional time to coordinate outreach effort and target audiences.

utterances.speaker: Annette Hill
utterances.text: Expand data sharing between agencies to increase text and email notifications.

utterances.speaker: Annette Hill
utterances.text: Adding information about deed theft, scams, predatory practices, and available prevention resources to lien sale notices.

utterances.speaker: Annette Hill
utterances.text: Increasing in-person and digital outreach to those who remain on the 10-day lease

utterances.speaker: Annette Hill
utterances.text: list to ensure additional touch points prior to the sale.

utterances.speaker: Annette Hill
utterances.text: The city is enhancing the payment and removal options to provide even more ways for homeowners to resolve their debts prior to the sale.

utterances.speaker: Annette Hill
utterances.text: to the sale, including expanding the water depth assistant, extending

utterances.speaker: Annette Hill
utterances.text: eligibility beyond homeowners with mortgage delinquencies to certain recipients of means-tested benefits,

utterances.speaker: Annette Hill
utterances.text: and individuals facing extenuating circumstances, including active duty military incarceration or employment.

utterances.speaker: Annette Hill
utterances.text: Expanding payment plan options for water and sewer debt.

utterances.speaker: Annette Hill
utterances.text: Pre-qualified low-income customers would have access to the same reduced interest rate payment agreements with DEP as they do with DOF.

utterances.speaker: Annette Hill
utterances.text: Expanding the Easy Exit, making the Easy Exit program more accessible to certain complex ownership structures such as LLCs and trusts.

utterances.speaker: Annette Hill
utterances.text: Protecting properties with deceased owners, removing properties from the lien sale for two years to allow ownership issues to be resolved,

utterances.speaker: Annette Hill
utterances.text: improving legal service referrals, streamlined referrals to the center of New York City neighborhoods for homeowners needing legal assistance.

utterances.speaker: Annette Hill
utterances.text: This administration and DOF are committed to administering all programs fairly and transparently.

utterances.speaker: Annette Hill
utterances.text: We're also committed to adhering to the council bill that was passed that removed predatory practices of lien sale

utterances.speaker: Annette Hill
utterances.text: and furthermore boost the outreach and programs that will maximize opportunities for New Yorkers who own their homes to keep their homes while insisting them with compliance.

chapters.summary: Sanchez notes that historically about 85% of properties are removed from the lien sale list, and asks if DOF has an anticipated removal rate for FY27. Hill says they are in planning stages and will share data when available.
chapters.title: Sanchez asks Hill about anticipated lien sale removal rate

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: And one last follow-up question here.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: On average, about 85% of properties are removed from the list in previous rounds of the lien sale.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Do you have an anticipated removal rate for FY27 based on the administration's analysis?

utterances.speaker: Annette Hill
utterances.text: At this point, we're just in the planning stages.

utterances.speaker: Annette Hill
utterances.text: We don't have any set data or set timeline for the lean sales, so I won't be able to give this information at this point.

utterances.speaker: Annette Hill
utterances.text: As soon as we have it, we'll be happy to share with the council.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Great.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Okay, I'm sure my colleagues will have further questions about the 2027 plans.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Thank you, and I'll now turn it over to Chair Lee.

chapters.summary: Lee asks about immediate recommendations to overcome barriers to Intro 1084. Shear says further conversations are needed, payment plans should be opt-in, and data collection could help assign the best plan, but they lack information on owner preferences.
chapters.title: Lee questions DOF on Intro 1084 barriers and opt-in vs opt-out

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: Okay, so I'll ask my first round of questions and then pass it on because we have a lot of council members who would like to ask questions.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: So this is more targeted on Intro 1084.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: So in 2025, DOF implemented 4,746 payment plans.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: 4,573 standard plans, 133 PT aid plans, and 40 reduced interest rate plans.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: Do I have the correct numbers?

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: Hopefully.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: Yes, you do, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: Okay, perfect.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: Okay, so I know that you had raised in your testimony some concerns about Intro 1084, and you had sort of outlined a few bullet points of some of the operational and technological

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: issues and things that would need to happen.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: So...

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: What are some of the immediate recommendations for those barriers, right?

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: So you outlined some of the barriers, but what would your recommendation be to if we wanted to move ahead with the plan?

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: My first recommendation would be that I think the council and the Department of Finance needs to have further conversations about the plan.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: So I can't give you a clear path.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: This is the way to move forward.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: I will just emphasize what I had mentioned in my testimony that

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: Selecting a plan based on the lowest total cost sounds straightforward, but it does increase the interest charges owed by the owner.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: Right, because it spreads it out, right?

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: So, like, it increases the time, which then increases the amount of interest.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: So part of this is discerning, well, is lowest cost referring to the total amount expended by the owner, which would include interest charges?

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: Is it referring to the installment payment?

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: That isn't clear, so we're not able to determine that.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: We offer a variety of payment plans, some of which have lower interest rates than others, so that we are being responsive to homeowners who are in...

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: Struggling in their financial situation.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: We don't know everything we need to know about owners in order to determine what plan they may be qualified for.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: And this is a bill that compels us to put them in the plan.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: We're not able to make that determination.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: And we are also concerned about placing owners in plans without their consent and how they may respond to that.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: And how that might leave them vulnerable to enforcement action in the future if due to their lack of consent, default on their payment plan.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: But let's just say that there was enough time where there was a concerted outreach effort to let folks know that this was happening if implemented, right?

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: What would you say is a sufficient amount of time, and what would the outreach look like?

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: And are you suggesting then that it should be an opt-in versus opt-out, or if you could speak a little bit to that?

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: Yes, we think.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: This is a good idea in terms of pushing us to be more proactive in getting people into payment plans.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: We do feel that payment plans should be opt-in.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: Rather than imposed on homeowners.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: And we think there are some interesting ideas here about how we may further increase our outreach efforts to get more struggling homeowners into payment plans.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: And then I know that you had mentioned...

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: You know, it's difficult for you to determine what type, you know, because every situation is different, every homeowner and their payment plans are different.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: So is there room to improve the data collection piece to help determine that, right?

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: So how are we better able to understand what the homeowner's needs are or what

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: position that they're in financially.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: Is it something that would simply be part of the application process when they first enroll, which would then give you a sense, a better sense of whether or not they could qualify for the automatic enrollment, if you could speak a little to that.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: We could certainly

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: incorporate that into the application process.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: There is certainly a lot of things that we do not know about property owners.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: People think that we know everything.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: And we do not.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: So one way to do that would be to have an application process where they're not having to

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: select which payment plan they're asking for, but they're providing the data for us so that we can assign or better yet suggest the best plan.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: But again,

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: And perhaps the one thing that we know the least about is how long of a payment plan do these owners want?

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: Because that has a major impact on both the installment payments as well as the accrued interest.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: And there isn't any data point that I know of that would tell us how long the homeowners want their payment plans to be for.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: Yeah, if there's a way where we could incorporate and get that data, that would definitely be helpful on your end as well.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: And because, you know, as you said, 20% down payment for the default, the lifeline, it could be a lot depending on how much is owed, right?

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: So not every homeowner may choose to do that or is financially able to do that.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: Yes, exactly.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: And, again, there is a wide range of delinquencies.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: There are some people who have been delinquent for just a couple of months, and they only owe a few hundred dollars.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: And there are others who owe a lot more and who are struggling more.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: And for the former group, we frankly don't think it makes sense to enroll them in the payment plan.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: And for the latter group, we very much want to and look forward to having constructive conversations with you about how we can best do that.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: And just based on the...

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: data and your records, existing records, which plan has the lowest total cost for each owner?

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: And you kind of went into that a little bit.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: I know it's hard to maybe look at the data based on what you have now collected, but based on what you have existing, what plan has the lowest total cost?

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: I can't really speak to that.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: I can just say that our PTA plans have the lowest interest.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: We have four different types of PTA plans.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: But then part of the challenge here is defining what is lowest cost.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: And then in terms of the upgrades that you spoke about that would be needed to implement such a program, including staffing, technical upgrades, what would you estimate the cost would be if we wanted to implement something like this?

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: We don't have an estimate available today, but we will work on getting that to you.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: Okay, great.

chapters.summary: Lee asks how many SCHE/DHE recipients have outstanding balances but are not enrolled in PTA. Shear says 3,859 properties have active benefits and outstanding taxes, and a report on debt size and age is coming in a couple of weeks.
chapters.title: Lee asks DOF about PTA enrollment and eligible non-participants

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: Okay, homeowners enrolled, just shifting to Skihi and Dihi, homeowners enrolled in Skihi and Dihi are automatically eligible for PTAID payment plans, which as long as the owner stays current on the payment plan, reduces the interest charged on the outstanding balance.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: This reduces the burden on low-income homeowners who are struggling to keep their homes, and it's a goal I think we all share.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: So we should have a goal to enroll every single Skihi and Dihi recipient with outstanding balances in a plan that lowers their interest rates.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: And so how many current Skihi and Dihi recipients have outstanding balances with the city but are not enrolled in PTA?

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: So there are 3,859 properties that have active she or the he benefits and outstanding property taxes.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: We are in the process of producing a report that will give further information on the size and the age of the debt, as well as the payment plan status of these owners.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: And when we have that, we will pass that along.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: Okay, great.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: Do you know how long it would take to get that?

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: No, we expect to have it within the next couple of weeks.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: Oh, okay, perfect.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: And just out of curiosity, why do you think there are folks that are eligible but not enrolled?

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: Is it lack of knowledge?

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: Eligible for PTA but not enrolled, sorry.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: Is it just a lack of not knowing about the program or not enough outreach?

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: It's a variety of things.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: Again, we love the PTA program.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: We were proud and pleased to create it with the hand in hand with the council.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: It does defer payment of taxes, which does increase the total amount that's due over time.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: For some people, that's perfect.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: It allows them to age in their homes and to stay in place.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: For others, however,

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: They may want to keep paying the full amount due to prevent interest from accruing.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: For others, it may be a lack of knowledge or a fear of doing business with the government.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: So we don't know, and that's why we're always open to working with the council on improving our outreach.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: Yeah, and we would love to partner and continue on that because there's a lot of homeowners, I think, in many of our districts that maybe are not, that are qualified and eligible but not enrolled.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: And is the information that DOF has,

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: as on file for she and he recipients sufficient to auto-enroll these homeowners into the PTA program?

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: Is that information that you would know?

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: We know more information.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: So we certainly know that their income level qualifies.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: But then, again, we think that we want to have their consent.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: We think that's important for people to buy in.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: And there are other things that we don't know.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: For example, how long they want their PTA agreement to run for.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: So it's a first step.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: It doesn't take you all of the way there.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: And we think further conversations are needed to determine how we can increase enrollment in

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: PTA than other Department of Finance payment plans.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: Okay.

chapters.summary: Lee asks about cost estimates for implementing Intro 1084 and data on late fees. Shear says no estimate yet, discusses quarterly delinquency notices (140k-150k) versus annual class 1 non-payers (14k), and clarifies that late payments incur interest, not penalties.
chapters.title: Lee asks DOF for cost estimates and late payment data

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: And speaking of the other programs, approximately how many households does DOF estimate to be eligible for the four proposed payment plan options under the bill?

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: We don't have an estimate.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: Again, the estimates that we make are very sensitive to the amount of debt that we're talking about.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: DOF, for example, we send quarterly delinquency notices.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: To property owners roughly in between each quarter of billing, so about 45 days after each billing, if they owe more than $100.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: Those notices, we end up producing about 140,000, 150,000 of those every quarter.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: But some of the debt is very young.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: When we look at an entire fiscal year and we say what is the number of class one homeowners

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: who have not fully paid their property taxes for that fiscal year, the number drops down to about 14,000.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: So that's a very wide disparity.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: So, again, that's why we're looking forward to having conversations with the council so we can decide on what are the different factors that go into determining

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: the target population here.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: And once we're able to do that, we'll be able to do that.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: able to provide you with a better estimate.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: Yeah, that's a big delta.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: Yeah, would love to get a sense of where all those folks fall in the middle.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: So, okay.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: And then just lastly, before I pass it on to Deputy Speaker Williams, from FI 25 to 26, how many individuals under each qualifying group were subject to late fees or paid their property taxes late?

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: So we don't, again, we don't have that number.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: It's really based on the response I just gave is

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: if we are looking at, for example, each quarter, everyone who owes more than $100 for any period, as little as 45 days, that's 140,000 to 150,000

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: taxpayers, including all property taxes.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: So how you specify that determines how large that group is.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: And also, just to be clear, people who are late with the property taxes do not receive penalties.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: They receive interest charges.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: And they know they're receiving these interest charges?

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: Yes, they do.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: We clearly delineate the interest in the bills that we send to them.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: And just a really quick follow-up question.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: If you have an ability to send out notices on the late interest payment amounts to those folks, then how much more involved would it be to then give them the information and notification about the auto-enrollment?

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: Plans.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: Some.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: Well, again, I think what's most important here is for the administration and the council to come together and decide on what is the population that we're targeting.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: Are we doing opt-in or are we compelling?

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: And what additional information do we need to receive from this population?

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: I think that needs to come first before we iron out the logistical details.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: I think if we can agree on who we're targeting, DOF can be constructive in suggesting how we can best notify them.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: Perfect.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: I have more follow-up questions about enrollment, or outreach, rather, but I'm going to pass it off now to Deputy Speaker Williams.

chapters.summary: Deputy Speaker Williams asks about the difference between the new Our Home term sheet and existing programs, and how many developers use them. Carrión discusses ANCP conversions, the dedicated Our Home term sheet, and Open Door pipeline, noting 150 units/year average and goal to double.
chapters.title: Williams questions Carrión on term sheets, Open Door production

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: I had a question about the term sheets you mentioned.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: I know that I thought there were some existing, I don't know if term sheets, but programs to convert apartments into homes and other financial tools to build home ownership.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: And so I just wanted to know what the difference would be with this new term sheet.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Versus the existing ones and how many people or developers actually leverage the

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: existing tools and what you project the number would be with the new tool, the new term sheet.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: So we have had both a specific program, and maybe you're thinking of ANCP, right, which is a conversion program for the buildings that used to be known as TIL.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: And so that has been going.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: I'm happy to share numbers with you in terms of how many we're seeing.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: It's probably on track.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: We've converted four TILs or ANCPs this year, and there's more that we think we'll be able to do this fiscal year.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: And then through our normal preservation pipeline, it's been something that you could come to us and say, well, we want to be a co-op.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: Is there a possibility of getting financing with a sponsor through our existing capital programs?

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: What's different about our home is that it's specifically dedicated just to this purpose and that it's got this target of doing 150 units per year for the next two years.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Did you work with developers and folks who are building home ownership to figure out the term sheets?

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Because in many conversations with them, they've always complained how not so good they are, which is why we don't see them using those term sheets and producing home ownership opportunities.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: It's very difficult.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: So I just...

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: I'm wondering, like, how are you addressing that issue?

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Because you could have the tool, but if no one finds the tool beneficial, then I don't know how you'll, like, meet the goal.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: So we have also heard.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: There's always consternation about whether the term sheets are rich enough, and we are constantly working to sort of address the market conditions that we're in at any given moment to make sure that our term sheets are usable.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: In our home conversations, we have consulted with those, particularly those who we know have an interest in being sponsors of conversion of limited equity co-ops.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: We're also weighing that against the need to make sure that our term sheet, in terms of when they do convert, has purchase prices that range, as I described earlier, from very low, 50% AMI,

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: to slightly higher incomes, particularly for vacancies.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: And that sort of mix of incomes will allow for...

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: Our capital to go further.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Can the term sheets also be used for new development, so not just conversions?

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: So that's the open door term sheet, which is the term sheet we use in order to build new construction.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Yeah, that's the one that most developers say.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: Oh, we have a big pipeline for open door.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: What are the numbers?

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: For current open door?

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: And how many people have used Open Door in the past?

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: So I don't have for you everything we've ever produced, but I can tell you now.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: So we've been doing about 150 units a year on average for the last three years, and this year we're on track to double that.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: So we're hoping to do 300 new construction units through Open Door.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: Fiscal year 27, and then again in fiscal year 28.

chapters.summary: Williams expresses concern that homeownership unit numbers are very low compared to overall development, and that developers prefer rentals because term sheets are not good for homeownership. Carrión offers to connect with developers who have issues.
chapters.title: Williams presses HPD on low homeownership unit numbers and term sheet issues

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Yeah, the numbers are...

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: It's just so low.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Like, for instance, with the Jamaica Neighborhood Plan, the projected number of units is 12,000, but the number of home ownership units is such a small percentage of the overall units.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: And so I'm just hoping that...

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: We find more ways for developers to leverage Open Door because it is such a small number.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Like those numbers personally from you are not impressive when you talk about like overall unit count in new development.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: And so I'm just hoping that we find more opportunities because most, for me, I only see those opportunities very rarely, if at all.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: And then when you do see them, it's typically on city-owned property because there's more.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Tools you can leverage to make the deal work.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: So yeah, that's just been the biggest thing.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: For me, when I talk to developers, they always say that the term sheets are not good for developing home ownership, which is why they prefer to develop rental units.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: I would be happy to have you refer anybody who has issue.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: I mean, generally speaking, right, again, our term sheets are pretty generous.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: I think open door goes up to $445,000 per unit in subsidy.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: All the homeownership opportunities in my district, they're on city-owned property.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: There's none on private-owned property.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Just from my experience.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: But I'm sure that there's a ton of questions.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: You'll do second round.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: I have more questions, but I'll stop there.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Deputy Speaker.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: So now I'm going to turn it over to Councilmember Joseph, followed by Narcisse.

chapters.summary: Councilmember Rita Joseph asks if HPD has specific targets for affordable homeownership in neighborhood plans like South of Prospect Park. Carrión says they will discuss mix, city-owned sites, and homeownership possibilities.
chapters.title: Joseph asks HPD about homeownership targets in neighborhood plans

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Good to see you, Commissioner.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: How are you?

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Along with my colleagues, we are doing the South of Prospect Park neighborhood plan with

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: DCP, we heard from long-term residents that they want their children to be able to buy homes in the community they grow up.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Does HPD have any specific target for delivering new affordable home ownership opportunities through its neighborhood plan?

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: In particular, community boards, for example, 1417?

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: Yeah, thank you very much for that question.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: I think as we continue to develop the neighborhood plan, I think this is a conversation we should continue to have.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: I think what we want to see out of a neighborhood plan, especially one of this scale, is going to be a mix on both the kind of private development that's not subsidized to make sure that there's a healthy mix of both rental and homeownership that's getting produced just in the general housing that's getting built as a result of the neighborhood plan.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: And then we're also looking at city-owned sites where we can add extra affordable housing and kind of adjust the mix of market rate and affordable housing.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: And on those city-owned sites, I think we'd be happy to have a conversation about homeownership and what's possible there.

chapters.summary: Joseph describes homeowners whose homes were damaged by adjacent construction, often older adults of color, and asks what HPD and DOB do. Carrión acknowledges the concern and says early intervention is needed; DOB representative says they will look into specific cases.
chapters.title: Joseph raises construction damage to adjacent homeowners, asks for HPD/DOB response

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Yeah, we would love to have that.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: In my district, Intro 1096, we have several instances where homeowners have had their home damaged from adjacent construction.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: These homeowners have been left holding the bags, damaged homes, either because developers disregard access agreements or fail to sign access agreements in the first place.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Homeowners consistently find that DOB fails to meaningfully protect their homes from this type of damage.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: These homeowners we find are often older adults, homeowners of color, who struggle to protect themselves from this behavior in court.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Is financial distress from disruptive construction practices a form of displaced pressure, the homeowners'advocacies?

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: So we've seen that.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: I have an older adult in my district who is squeezing, someone is squeezing a building in between two homes.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: And they damage her.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: property?

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: What is HPD, DOB, what is the plan for when these things happen?

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: So I don't want to speak for DOB, but I believe they're here.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: But speaking for HPD, I do think this is a legitimate concern.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: And again, our desire to build as much affordable housing on every vacant piece of land that we can should not disrupt existing homeowners or tenants, frankly.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: And we need to make sure that that isn't happening.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: Again, being made aware of it early so that we can take intervention.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: We very much want to make sure, again, that while we're building and trying to meet our goals of 200,000 units over the next 10 years, we are not at the same time disrupting or displacing anybody as a result.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Displacing and safety, not just displacing, but this is generational wealth for communities of color.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: And when someone comes in and destroys it with no, there's no payment, nothing, you leave someone holding the bag.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: So this is something I'm seeing often across the city and particularly in my district that I would love to see addressed in real time, not a month or year or six months later.

chapters.summary: Joseph raises complaints from homeowners in Kensington about DOB enforcement on HVAC units installed before they purchased. DOB says they are looking into it, need permits, and will follow up with specific addresses.
chapters.title: Joseph questions DOB on HVAC violations for pre-existing alterations

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: My final question, in the past couple of months for Intro 1097, I've been contacted by a community in Kensington, predominantly Jewish homeowners, who report that they've been getting a lot of DOB enforcement on HVAC units that were...

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: The alteration was done before they purchased the homes.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: So they've been getting a lot of ticketing.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Meanwhile,

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: What can we do to protect homeowners who bought homes that already had alterations before they purchased the homes?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: To be sworn in.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: Have to be sworn in.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Please raise your right hand.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Do you swear?

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Do you affirm to tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth before these committees and to respond honestly to council member questions?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: So on the issue of HVAC units, thank you for bringing that up.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: That's actually something that we're hearing citywide.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: We're starting to hear that issue.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: So these HVAC units, the mini splits, they require permits to install.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: So that's something we're actively looking into.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: So if you have specific addresses where this issue is coming from.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: I have a ton of them.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: Please, we'll reach out to you right after they hear.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Yes, please do.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: That's an issue that we're thinking through right now.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: Certainly, we need to do more outreach to property owners so that they understand that these devices need to be installed with proper permits.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: But absolutely intervening as soon as possible is key.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: But what about the ones that bought it already like that, didn't know that it was in a violation?

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Now they're racking up violations not knowing this was done to their homes.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Is there anything in place to support these homeowners?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: We'll look into the specific instances, but for smaller properties, we do have programs in place that allow them to correct violating conditions before they incur monetary penalties.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: But again, earliest intervention is key there because they have to correct within a certain time period in order to benefit from it.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Is DOB tracking that?

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Is there some way you're keeping that data?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: We're starting to compile it, this issue.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: It was just flagged for us last week is when we started looking into it because we're starting to hear from council members and community members about this issue.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: So we definitely need to meet in that community in my district so we can talk to these homeowners.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: I would love that.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: Thank you, Councilmember Joseph.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: I'd like to acknowledge that we've been joined by Councilmembers Hutton, Zhuang, and Brewer.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: And next up, we have Councilmember Narcisse, followed by Councilmember Brooks-Powers.

chapters.summary: Narcisse asks about property tax disparities between neighborhoods and deed theft complaints in Brooklyn. Shear says DOF is working on property tax reform legislation, has no community board breakdown for deed theft, but the office has received 300 referrals citywide.
chapters.title: Narcisse questions DOF on property tax disparities and deed theft complaints

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: And Madam Commissioner, I appreciate the fact that I think we're almost on the same page when it comes to housing.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: The mayor's housing plan says homeowners in Canarsie, East New York, and Cambria Heights pay effective property tax rates about twice what Park Slope and East Village homeowners pay.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: What specific change will DOF make to fix that on what timeline we're working on?

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: DOF is currently working with City Hall on property tax reform, and we are hoping to have legislation for the upcoming state legislative session.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: We are going to be on a good page, I hope.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Deed death has been heavily concentrated in black and brown communities, Caribbean communities in Brooklyn.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: How many complaints has the Office of Deed Death, do you know, Deed Death Prevention received in Brooklyn?

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: And from what community, specifically Community Board 18?

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: We don't have a breakdown by community board.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: We know that since the office was established, it's received more than 300 deed theft referrals.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: We will get to you the number for the community board or for your district.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

chapters.summary: Narcisse asks if HPD has analyzed whether loss of short-term rental income leads to tax arrears or mortgage defaults, and why homeowners face fines for short-term rentals but not long-term basement rentals. Carrión says no specific analysis, acknowledges tension, and will follow up.
chapters.title: Narcisse asks about short-term rental income loss and ADU rules

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Has HPD or the Office of the Homeowner Advocate ever looked at data at whether losing short-term rental income has led to tax arrears or mortgage defaults?

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Do you have any idea?

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: Yeah, so I don't think we've done that specific analysis.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: I know that there is a homeowner group out in the communities that are saying that they rely on short-term rentals in order to both not only cover their taxes but also their mortgage.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: I don't think we've done that specific analysis, but could certainly talk internally as to whether or not that is an analysis that we could sort of ride at.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Look into it because black and brown folks are losing their home left and right, and it's not a privilege.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: It's hard work, sweat, blood.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: The mayor's house plans support ADUs and basement units as income for homeowners.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Why should a homeowner who lives in the house be allowed to rent a basement long-term but face heavy fines for...

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: renting a spare room for short term?

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: Yeah, I think that's an interesting question.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: I would argue, you know, there has been obviously a lot of discussion about how short term rentals actually take away affordable housing in the city.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: I do think the point you're raising, which is sort of the other side of that argument, which is owner occupants who have either room or an ancillary unit.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: And benefit from the income that that produces is one of the sort of tensions that exists with trying to make sure short-term rentals aren't displacing long-term renters in the same community.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: So happy to follow up with you directly on this question to figure out if there is sort of a balance to be struck in terms of...

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: I appreciate you.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: And data has not changed really for the time that we stopped short-term rental to a mod unit in the market because those are home, one to two families home or one family.

chapters.summary: Narcisse asks if the administration supports her bill, Intro 1091. DOB says they are supportive of the intent to provide notice that a DOB violation could become a property lien, and want to discuss additional notice requirements.
chapters.title: Narcisse asks DOB if they support Intro 1091

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Last one, I'm going to say, do you have any problem?

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Do you support my bill?

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Administration support 1091.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: You have no problem with my bill?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: I think we're...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: I don't...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Sorry, that's you?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Oh, good.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: We're certainly supportive of the intent of the bill, which is to provide notice to homeowners that a DOB-issued violation could ultimately become a property lien.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: So currently such a warning doesn't exist in our violations.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: We're 100% supportive of taking a look at that, revising our violations to provide that earliest in time notice.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: What we'd like to discuss further is the additional notice requirements to understand if there are gaps, and if so, how do we address them?

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Okay, let me know, because I'm here to hope to help homeowners, because I know what a black and brown community have to go through to own a little property in New York City.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: And especially in the plan of New York City, the flood zone should be looking carefully for development, because as we saw what happened on Flatbush Avenue, we don't want all of us to be in the water.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: And the basement that we have that's sinking, I haven't seen any plan on that note.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: So we're going to look further.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: I'm going to talk to you guys because we have to have a plan because people, but the home, knowing that developers are gone and they're dealing with sinking home.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: So thank you for your time, and I have to pass it to my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Appreciate you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: Thank you, Councilmember Narcisse.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: I'd now like to turn it over to Councilmember Brooks Powers, followed by Salam.

chapters.summary: Brooks-Powers asks how many HCV holders are enrolled and closed on homes in the last five years, and how many first-time homebuyers received Home First assistance by borough. Carrión reports 162 active HCV participants, 5 closings in 2024-25, 171 Home First families last year, with breakdown by borough.
chapters.title: Brooks-Powers questions HPD on HCV homeownership and Home First data

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: I'm going to start with a couple of questions on my bill, and I just ask in your response to leave me a little bit of time to ask some district-specific questions.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: So in terms of Intro 861, the voucher homeownership outreach, I wanted to get a sense, Commissioner, in terms of how does HPD,

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: well, excuse me, how many HPD voucher holders are currently enrolled in the Housing Choice Voucher Homeownership Program and how many...

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: closed on a home in each of the last five years.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: And then regarding intro 862, how many first-time home buyers received home first assistance in each of the last five fiscal years?

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: And how do those numbers break down by borough?

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Does HPD track where applicants who were approved but never closed were trying to buy?

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: And with Intro 862, it would require HPD to assist at least 600 first-time homebuyers a year.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: What are the biggest barriers to getting there today?

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Outreach, the application and closing process, or the capacity of the nonprofit counseling partners?

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: So I'm going to try to remember those.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: I'll repeat whatever you want.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: So we'll start with the Housing Choice Voucher Program.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: It is, you know, less utilization than we'd like for the reasons I sort of spoke about in my testimony.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: Right now there's 162 active participants who receive housing choice vouchers through HPD who are actively trying to get to the place where they can purchase a home and convert the voucher.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: There were a total of five closings for that population.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: between, I think, calendar year 24 and 25.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: So that was your first question.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: I think your second question was on down payment assistance.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: The first?

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: So for home...

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: First, the past fiscal year, we served 171 families.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: And again, the goal is by 2028, fiscal year 2028, to be getting to at least 300 households with the down payment assistance.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: I think you asked, did you ask for a type of unit or type?

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: Or by borough.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: I wanted to know the number breakdown by borough in terms of how many first-time homebuyers received that assistance.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: So for that 171, which is the last completed fiscal year, it's pretty evenly split across the five boroughs.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: There were 45 coming from Brooklyn, 37 coming from the Bronx, 31 coming from...

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: from Queens, 29 coming from both Staten Island and an additional 21, sorry, 29 from Manhattan.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: And if at another time you could give me the full picture in terms of the five fiscal years, that'd be great.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: Yeah, we can go back to the beginning of the program for sure.

chapters.summary: Brooks-Powers asks about barriers to reaching 600 homebuyers annually and raises concerns about high foreclosure rates in her district. Carrión cites rising interest rates and maintenance fees, and discusses foreclosure prevention funding and targeted outreach.
chapters.title: Brooks-Powers asks about barriers to 600 homebuyers and district foreclosure concerns

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: And then the follow-up for 862 was it requires HPD chairs.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: I just asked for just a few more moments, if that's okay.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Would require HPD to assist at least 600 first-time homebuyers a year.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: What are the biggest barriers?

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Just wanted to understand that.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: So as I described, I think a $100,000 grant is a very generous down payment assistance.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: Just by comparison, the state offers its own version through Sunny May, which is only $15,000.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: So that change, which we upped from $40,000 to $100,000, has been really helpful in making higher utilization rates for the program.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: I would say today the challenge, the most significant challenge right now, is that rising interest rates.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: So when you go to get a mortgage, you are now looking at close to 7%, which is significantly higher than over the last, I would say, 12 years.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: While I was at Sunny May, interest rates were hovering below 5%.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: So it's a significant increase, and it makes the affordability much, much more challenging.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: The second big challenge is just how much it costs in terms of you're buying a co-op or a condo unit.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: Monthly HOA or maintenance fees continue to go up.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: That is the same reason that rental, there are

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: in the rental market because these buildings are dealing with rising interest, sorry, taxes, insurance probably most foremost.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: So it is making it, even if you can kind of afford the purchase price, to know that you can afford the ongoing monthly maintenance fee can be very challenging for low and moderate income prospective homebuyers.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: And I'm just going to close with the questions regarding my district.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: So first, District 31 saw 329 foreclosure filings last year, about 17% of all filings in Queens.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: When HPD runs outreach to buyers and existing owners, how does it connect distressed neighborhoods to counseling and legal help?

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: And then for the Department of Finance, tax liens sold on small homes in my district went from 44 in 2021 to 102 in 2025, more than doubling, while citywide.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: They rose by a little over half.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: What explains that concentration and what outreach did the Department of Finance do in Southeast Queens before the last sale?

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: And I'll just color it by saying I'm extremely concerned about the upcoming lien sale that is coming right now in light of.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: All of the affordability dynamics that exist today, and the fact that the foreclosure number in Southeast Queens is the highest, not only in Queens, but in the city, in my district, in the neighborhood.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: And so I'm extremely concerned and ringing the bells right now in terms of the need for much more targeted outreach and funding that the council had approved for this effort for my district in particular.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: I'll be very quick so we can hear from Department of Finance.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: But I do want to say, right, our foreclosure prevention funding, which is $4 million that the council provides, goes to this very large network of legal service providers and housing counseling groups.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: The housing counseling groups can work with homebuyers to potentially get a mortgage modification to get out of foreclosure, and legal services represents them during a foreclosure as, you know, counsel.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: There is also, as you know, the Homeowner Protection Program, which runs sort of simultaneous, which funding comes from the state.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: It's $40 million, of which $14 million comes to New York City to support about 30 of the HOP organizations.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: So while I completely hear what you're saying, and we do see signs of foreclosure distress very concentrated in neighborhoods like yours, we do have the ability to be very targeted.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: The other thing that we know is that the Center for New York City Neighborhoods gets direct access to the 90-day foreclosure

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: notice that DFS provides, which is the best way for us to get early outreach to very, very specifically address-level targeting because we know which folks are actually facing a potential foreclosure.

chapters.summary: Annette Hill responds to Brooks-Powers' concerns about lien sale outreach in Southeast Queens. She says they will share the at-risk list early, expand data sharing, and work with all districts, but does not commit to additional funding for her district.
chapters.title: Hill responds on lien sale outreach and funding for Southeast Queens

utterances.speaker: Annette Hill
utterances.text: Hi.

utterances.speaker: Annette Hill
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: Annette Hill
utterances.text: We forgot to the...

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Sorry, and if you could be brief, we have a lot of council members signed up.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Annette Hill
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Annette Hill
utterances.text: Well, the main thing for the outreach, we plan to share the outreach list with our nonprofit partners early in the 90-day process so they could start planning the outreach in the various districts.

utterances.speaker: Annette Hill
utterances.text: We also will be expanding data sharing between the agencies to make sure we get emails and text notifications to the owners on the 90-day list.

utterances.speaker: Annette Hill
utterances.text: Right now, like I said, we will be planning our extensive outreach as we move forward with planning the...

utterances.speaker: Annette Hill
utterances.text: The upcoming lien sale.

utterances.speaker: Annette Hill
utterances.text: We don't have anything to share now, but we are putting that into part of our planning process.

utterances.speaker: Annette Hill
utterances.text: If we got to the increase between 2021 and 2025, there was a four-year difference in when we had the lien sale.

utterances.speaker: Annette Hill
utterances.text: So all tax classes did show an increase in at-risk properties.

utterances.speaker: Annette Hill
utterances.text: Because there was a four-year gap between the lien sale.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Can you commit to additional funding for my district since we're leading the nation in foreclosures?

utterances.speaker: Annette Hill
utterances.text: We will be reaching out to all districts, including your district, to ensure everyone gets the outreach that's needed.

utterances.speaker: Annette Hill
utterances.text: We will definitely...

utterances.speaker: Annette Hill
utterances.text: I'll definitely put it on about your district, but we will be working with all the district council members to ensure we reach all at-risk residents.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Thank you, Councilmember Brooks-Powers.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Councilmember Justin Sanchez, followed by...

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Followed by Wong.

chapters.summary: Councilmember Justin Sanchez asks how HPD balances permanent affordability with homeownership as a pathway to the middle class, and how much equity a typical owner gains. Carrión discusses the tension, mentioning a 2.5% annual equity allowance.
chapters.title: Justin Sanchez questions HPD on resale restrictions and equity building

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Thank you, Chairs.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Hello, everyone.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Good to see you.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Resale restrictions limit how much equity a family can build.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: How does HPD balance permanent affordability against homeownership as a pathway to the middle class?

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: How much equity does a typical open-door or CLT owner gain after 10 years?

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: So I would make a distinction between CLTs and a program like Open Door, which don't run exactly the same way.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: You are naming a very real tension, I think, that I personally struggle with, which is we want homeowners who are getting access to first-time homeownership to be able to make earned equity.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: As generations before them have.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: We also want to be mindful that if we don't put some resale restrictions, then that unit leaves the affordable housing homeownership market and we have to pay a lot of money to build new ones to replace it.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: So finding a balance between those two things is constantly on our minds and something that we debate pretty robustly internally.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: We are right now coming up with maybe some changes to how we will find that balance.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: I think historically there's been about a 2.5% equity allowance every year.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: So if you stay in the home for 10 years, you've built.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: both bought down your mortgage principal, but you're also able to sell for a 2.5% increase for every year you've lived in the home.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: So I would say, you know, we're looking now to see if we think those numbers are still correct, whether they need editing, but we do work constantly to find the balance between equity building and also preserved affordability.

chapters.summary: Sanchez asks what a family at 80% AMI can afford with Home First assistance, and about HPD's average subsidy per unit. Carrión explains the 35% debt-to-income cap, average subsidy of $85,000, capped at $100,000.
chapters.title: Justin Sanchez asks about affordability at 80% AMI and HPD subsidy per unit

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: In today's market, what can a family at 80% AMI actually afford to buy with the current levels of home first assistance and where in the city?

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: If funding were held flat or increased by 25%, how many families would we add or cut?

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: I'm going to need you to repeat the second half on the first half.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: I mean, I could pull out a mortgage calculator and tell you exactly.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: So I don't have, like, with me what is 50%.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: But the way we consider affordability when we're thinking about homeownership is debt-to-income ratio.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: So what we're looking at is a 35% cap.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: For the debt to income, your housing debt to income.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: So that factors property taxes, insurance, mortgage payments, and if you're in a co-op or a condo, your maintenance payments.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: We don't want any of that to be more than 35% of your gross monthly income.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: And so we set sales prices based on what we think a potential homeowner can afford in order to back into a monthly payment and then layer in the other factors to make sure it's affordable.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: So we have different sales prices for people at 50, 80, 100, and so forth.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: So could you explain a little bit if so for HPD subsidy program program?

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: like open door.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: What is HPD's average subsidy per unit and how does it change as you go deeper into affordability?

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: So it's capped at $100,000 per homeowner.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: The average historically has been close to about $85,000.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: And again, we're backing into that to get to that 35% debt to income ratio when factoring in things like maintenance, property taxes, and insurance.

chapters.summary: Sanchez asks about demand for the HomeFix program compared to funding, and wait times for homeowners with failing roofs or boilers. Carrión says there is no waitlist, capacity exists, average time is 6-8 months, and they are working on efficiencies.
chapters.title: Justin Sanchez asks about HomeFix demand and wait times

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: For the HomeFix program, what is the current demand compared to the available funding?

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Is there a wait list, and how long is the wait for a homeowner whose roof or boiler is currently failing?

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: So there isn't a wait list, and there is capacity within the program.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: We have found that we need to sort of tighten the processes around HomeFix in order to make it go more quickly.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: The average time is probably taking, I would say, between six and eight months from the time that they apply.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: Part of that is that we have to work with the homeowner to scope the work, right, to sort of figure out exactly what needs to be done, and then identify contractors, which the homeowners can select.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: So we are working to sort of make more efficiencies.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: This program is also run through a partnership with the Center for New York City Neighborhoods and Neighborhood Restore.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: And I think, you know, we are hoping to see growth within that program so we can get to more homeowners.

chapters.summary: Sanchez asks how HPD monitors compliance with regulatory agreements, how many violations were found, and what penalties or clawbacks are used. Carrión describes the asset management team, annual reporting, ability to declare default, and revoke Article 11.
chapters.title: Justin Sanchez questions HPD on compliance monitoring and penalties

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
