utterances.text: When developers receive city subsidies, just changing lanes really quick, when developers receive city subsidies or tax breaks, how does HPD monitor compliance with these regulatory agreements?

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: does monitor how many violations did it find last year, and when a company ignores its obligations, what penalties or clawbacks does the city use, and how much has it recovered?

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: So I think the recovery question I want to explore with you a little bit, but you're asking, right, how do we oversee all of the housing that we subsidize?

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: So that is done primarily through our asset management team.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: So we have a whole division that is asset and property management.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: Anybody who gets a subsidy loan from HPD or an Article 11 has to report to us annually on their financial situation, on compliance, and on the physical conditions within the building.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: We do have the ability to declare a default under our regulatory agreements if we can't get an owner to come into compliance.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: And we also have the ability to pursue revocation of an Article 11 if there is serious noncompliance.

chapters.summary: Sanchez asks what happens to tenants who don't want to buy or can't afford to buy when a rental building converts to a co-op. Carrión says no 100% consensus needed, a majority vote, and non-purchasing tenants can stay as rent-stabilized tenants.
chapters.title: Justin Sanchez asks about tenants who don't buy in co-op conversions

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: One last question.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Finally, when a rental building converts to a co-op through Our Home or ANCP, what happens to tenants who don't want to buy or can't afford to buy?

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: How does HPD keep the co-op financially stable when a share of units remain rentals?

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: And has it explored other mixed models?

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: It's a great question, and the answer is yes.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: We do have a process in both ANCP, and we haven't launched our home yet, but when we do, there will be a process by which you do not need 100% consensus from the residents in order to convert to co-op.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: So we would be looking for a majority of residents in advance of...

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: say moving through with our home, that there is a majority, probably an 80% or so majority, want to be shareholders.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: Whether some folks can't or just choose not to purchase, they would be able to stay as rent-stabilized tenants.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Thank you, Councilmember Justin Sanchez, a.k.a.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Primo.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Now I'd like to turn it over to Councilmember Wong, followed by Wilson.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: And I need to acknowledge that we've been joined by Councilmember Ressler.

chapters.summary: Councilmember Phil Wong asks about the citywide problem of homeowners fined for split HVAC units installed without permits. DOB says they are looking into it and will follow up. Wong also asks about co-op board training; Carrión describes the UHAB contract with 180 classes/year.
chapters.title: Wong questions DOB on HVAC violations and HPD on co-op board training

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: I have a question about the split HVAC units.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: This appears to be a citywide problem, and certainly in my district we have

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: hundreds and hundreds of homeowners install these dual units and only for years, they've been using it for years, some of them using for decades, and now suddenly

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: they're slapped with fines that you installed it without a permit or you installed it without the proper paperwork.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: And my question is that,

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Most of them don't even know they need permits.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: They see it as, they don't, they see it, well, why do I need the permit if I have a window unit, you know, upstairs, and why do I need a permit for this?

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: So what is being done to address this?

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Because certainly in my district, the homeowners are just confused and outraged.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: But these fines are into thousands of dollars.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Please answer that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: Something that we just recently started looking into because it's been brought to our attention by council members, community members.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: We're certainly pulling together all that information.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: If you have specific addresses that are on your radar, please share them with us.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: We'll follow up with your office after the hearing.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Dozens.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: We have homes that install multiple of these split units, and their fines are several thousand dollars.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: And I only get only a small set of these phone calls because they don't even know.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Many of them bought homes without knowing that these units are in violation.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: Again, it's an issue that we're just very recently looking into, but we suspect that folks are calling in 311 complaints, which is prompting DOB to visit the locations, and that's how we find that the devices were installed without permits.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Isn't that the contractor's job?

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Or when I buy one, let's say I buy one of these.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: It's the seller's job.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: They should make sure that they're pulling permits, but it seems that perhaps homeowners are not aware that permits are required or they're not working with the contractor to determine whether they're pulling permits.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: So on our end, we're certainly thinking through how to communicate to homeowners that they need to have permits to install these devices.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: We'll definitely be planning for outreach, but if there's any specific locations, please let us know because the earliest that we can intervene, the better to avoid additional penalties being imposed.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: Some of these, if they're issued as Class 1 violations, they prompt re-inspections, and then penalties begin to snowball, so it's something we definitely want to intervene early on.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: On a follow-up question, co-op, co-op board members training, Bill 406.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Co-op boards, the qualities vary.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Some are very well run, some are not.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: My question is, well, right now, before this bill, how are co-op boards trained?

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Let's say I just joined a co-op board.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Where do I get my training right now?

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: So as I mentioned in my testimony, we have a $7 million contract with the Urban Homesteading Assistance Board to serve all HDFCs in the city, both those that are regulated by HPD, but also those that are just in existence and are potentially benefiting from the damp tax cap.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: They do, under this contract, about 180 training classes a year that are open to all HDFC shareholders and board members.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: And then they do individual co-op trainings with shareholders and boards at specific sites, about 220 hours of individual training per month every year under that contract.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: May I have a follow-up question?

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Yeah, really.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: I know co-op boys that get sued all the time.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Can you talk about the liability issue?

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: What if you train co-op members and they don't do their job or they sit on a board that doesn't do anything?

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: And you trained them, so what's the liability?

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: I actually don't do the training, but yes, our partners at Urban Homesteading Assistance Board does do the training.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: I'm not totally familiar with what specific liability issues you're talking about.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: But again, if there is a co-op or a board that is struggling to issue proper financial...

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: requirements or to communicate with the shareholders or not functioning from a governance perspective, we would ask you have to go out and start working with that co-op board.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Okay, thank you.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Thank you, Jim.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Thank you, Councilmember Wong.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: So far, you are the best behaved.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Councilmember Wilson, followed by Councilmember Mealy.

chapters.summary: Councilmember Carl Wilson asks about HPD's strategy for permanently affordable homeownership in high-cost neighborhoods like Chelsea and Hell's Kitchen. Carrión discusses limited equity co-ops, community land trusts, and 1,200 units financed since 2020.
chapters.title: Wilson asks HPD about permanently affordable homeownership in high-cost areas

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: In neighborhoods like Chelsea and Hell's Kitchen, the ones that I represent, things like down payment assistance alone may not bridge the gap between what households can afford and what homes cost.

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: What is HPD's strategy to create permanently affordable homeownership in more high-cost neighborhoods?

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: And does that include things like limited equity cooperatives?

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: So that's traditionally all that we build through the program like open door, right?

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: These are limited equity.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: There is some opportunity for equity building, as we described a moment ago, 2.5%, but we balance that in order to achieve long-term affordability.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: The other mechanism that we're now using a lot of is working with our community land trust partners, where there is a commitment to permanent affordability through 99-year ground leases.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: Since 2020, we have worked to finance 1,200 units on community land trusts that then benefit from that permanent affordability.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: I don't have the exact breakdown, but the vast majority of the units that we've worked with on CLTs has been for...

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: Homeownership.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: That's both single family and co-ops.

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: And for those CLT projects, where are they mostly located?

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: I mean, we have a lot of CLTs now.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: I would say we have more than one potentially in many neighborhoods, but it's great.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: It's a very large network.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: There's a group called the Nicely Coalition.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: You know, the oldest one being Cooper Square, which I'm sure you're familiar with them.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: So, you know, we don't actually create limited equity co-ops.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: They sort of come into existence and then we work to support them.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: But I would say at the moment, and I'm trying to think, I actually don't know if there's one squarely working in Chelsea or in the neighborhood you're speaking of, but we do have a large, large network of limited, sorry, CLTs, community land trusts, forming across the city.

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: And then about existing affordable co-ops.

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: So something like Penn South, which is Article 5, limited equity co-op.

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: I'm sure you've heard me talk about them before here.

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: That demonstrates the value of preserving affordable cooperatives over ownership over generations.

chapters.summary: Wilson asks how HPD identifies financial distress in HDFCs and other limited equity co-ops early, and helps before unaffordable maintenance increases. Carrión says regulated co-ops report annually, and a new RFP will bring technical assistance for Mitchell Lama co-ops.
chapters.title: Wilson asks how HPD identifies financial distress in co-ops

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: For HDFCs and other limited equity co-ops, how do you identify, or for both agencies really, how do you identify financial distress early,

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: whether from tax arrears, insurance costs, or major repairs or system upgrades?

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: And help with assistance before the residents face unaffordable maintenance increases.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: Yeah, it is challenging.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: For the ones that we finance, so right, of the HDFCs, sometimes we actually have capital dollars or a mortgage in the project, and sometimes we don't.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: For those that we do finance, they do have the same obligation to report to us annually, their financial statements, their...

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: Physical conditions, their compliance with our regulatory agreement.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: So that would be a way for us to know for that portion of the co-ops that exist, early indications of distress.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: Similarly with the Mitchell Lama co-ops, they have obligations to report to us if they are city subsidized, I'm sorry, city supervised Mitchell Lamas.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: I do think we have more to do here, which is why I mentioned in my testimony we've just launched a new RFP to bring on technical assistance providers.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: specifically to work with Mitchell Lama Cooperatives, where we know there is a lot of distress.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Councilmember Wilson.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: I'd now like to call on Councilmember Mealy, followed by Joanne.

chapters.summary: Councilmember Darlene Mealy describes a homeowner whose property was damaged by adjacent construction and then charged $3 million by HPD, which became a lien on their property tax. Carrión says HPD does not have a database on such cases and will look into specific examples.
chapters.title: Mealy confronts HPD on construction damage and liens charged to homeowners

utterances.speaker: Darlene Mealy
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Darlene Mealy
utterances.text: Hi, Commissioner.

utterances.speaker: Darlene Mealy
utterances.text: I feel it's kind of disingenuous, but my colleague just asked you about when your department, HPD,

utterances.speaker: Darlene Mealy
utterances.text: have contractors building and hurt homeowners next to their property, their foundation is, and you said it's nothing that y'all could do right now.

utterances.speaker: Darlene Mealy
utterances.text: How could that, you just said assessment manager, how many defaults have happened to this day that y'all did something about any of those developments that hurt another homeowner that y'all was doing

utterances.speaker: Darlene Mealy
utterances.text: building homes?

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: So, sorry if I was misunderstood.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: I don't think there's nothing we can do.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: But I do want to say for buildings that are in existence, that is where HPD has oversight for code violations.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: If it's an active construction site, it would be more within DOBs.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: DOB?

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: Supervision.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: But again, regardless, I think both agencies care very deeply about making sure that while we are trying to build more affordable housing.

utterances.speaker: Darlene Mealy
utterances.text: Do you have a database on it?

utterances.speaker: Darlene Mealy
utterances.text: How many homes been damaged?

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: We do not have a database on it.

utterances.speaker: Darlene Mealy
utterances.text: Why?

utterances.speaker: Darlene Mealy
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: Darlene Mealy
utterances.text: That is taking away black and brown home ownership that's been in our communities.

utterances.speaker: Darlene Mealy
utterances.text: And why I'm saying that, because now with DOF here, just as well, it leads right into it.

utterances.speaker: Darlene Mealy
utterances.text: HPD.

utterances.speaker: Darlene Mealy
utterances.text: You have a...

utterances.speaker: Darlene Mealy
utterances.text: A bill will come in, and then you're charged a homeowner.

utterances.speaker: Darlene Mealy
utterances.text: Then it'll go to their property tax.

utterances.speaker: Darlene Mealy
utterances.text: And that's where Department of Finance come in.

utterances.speaker: Darlene Mealy
utterances.text: So I have a homeowner.

utterances.speaker: Darlene Mealy
utterances.text: Now their bill is $3 million.

utterances.speaker: Darlene Mealy
utterances.text: It just keeps going.

utterances.speaker: Darlene Mealy
utterances.text: So I looked at all their things.

utterances.speaker: Darlene Mealy
utterances.text: HPD charged them for knocking down a demolition of something in which it was only because y'all were building next door to their house, and then their

utterances.speaker: Darlene Mealy
utterances.text: foundation was unstable, and then y'all taxing this man.

utterances.speaker: Darlene Mealy
utterances.text: Millions now.

utterances.speaker: Darlene Mealy
utterances.text: And so I start looking to see what department do we go to and guess what?

utterances.speaker: Darlene Mealy
utterances.text: It's no department that could tell you who was putting these fines on these properties.

utterances.speaker: Darlene Mealy
utterances.text: Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: The issue of construction.

utterances.speaker: Darlene Mealy
utterances.text: It's really from HPD.

utterances.speaker: Darlene Mealy
utterances.text: It come from HPD, didn't go to Department of Finance, and it's on people property taxes.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: Councilmember Wright, you may be talking about ERP liens.

utterances.speaker: Darlene Mealy
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: Darlene Mealy
utterances.text: Just regular, everyday problems that y'all created.

utterances.speaker: Darlene Mealy
utterances.text: On a homeowner that their building is next door.

utterances.speaker: Darlene Mealy
utterances.text: Their foundation is now messed up.

utterances.speaker: Darlene Mealy
utterances.text: And now you're charging a homeowner.

utterances.speaker: Darlene Mealy
utterances.text: And this is not just one or two.

utterances.speaker: Darlene Mealy
utterances.text: This is a lot.

utterances.speaker: Darlene Mealy
utterances.text: She just asked you, and you said, y'all don't have a database or anything.

utterances.speaker: Darlene Mealy
utterances.text: That's concerning.

utterances.speaker: Darlene Mealy
utterances.text: That is our taxpayers, homeowners that need to keep their homes.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: It would be helpful to look into the specific examples that you're referencing.

utterances.speaker: Darlene Mealy
utterances.text: That's only one of them, but it's disingenuous for y'all to just say y'all don't have a database on that.

utterances.speaker: Darlene Mealy
utterances.text: That is people homes you're messing with.

utterances.speaker: Darlene Mealy
utterances.text: And they don't have the money to get lawyers to fight y'all.

utterances.speaker: Darlene Mealy
utterances.text: So I guess we are their voices.

utterances.speaker: Darlene Mealy
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Councilmember Mealy.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: In the audience, you cannot interrupt the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: If you agree, you can shake your hands, all of that.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: But please, no audible.

utterances.speaker: Darlene Mealy
utterances.text: And I thank you, Deputy Commissioner.

utterances.speaker: Darlene Mealy
utterances.text: I feel that you at least understand that 1084.

utterances.speaker: Darlene Mealy
utterances.text: You can't just put that on homeowners, you know, put them in a plan that they did not agree on.

utterances.speaker: Darlene Mealy
utterances.text: So I would love to talk.

utterances.speaker: Darlene Mealy
utterances.text: to you in regards to that because that's how government's supposed to work with community and homeowners.

utterances.speaker: Darlene Mealy
utterances.text: So kudos to you.

utterances.speaker: Darlene Mealy
utterances.text: I'm looking forward to see more of that.

utterances.speaker: Darlene Mealy
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Thank you, Councilmember Mealy.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: We'll now go to Councilmember Zhuang, followed by Councilmember Brewer.

chapters.summary: Councilmember Susan Zhuang asks if co-op board training can be provided virtually, and raises concerns about property tax disparities where less wealthy districts pay higher rates. Carrión says training is both in-person and virtual; DOF says they are working on property tax reform.
chapters.title: Zhuang asks about virtual training and property tax disparities

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Thank you, Chairs, and thank you, Commissioner, to be here.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: I have a couple questions.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: The first question, give that board members live all over the city and some older adults living in outermost parts will be trained.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Will this training be provided virtually?

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I want to make sure I understand your question.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: Council member, you're asking for co-operators.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: Can they be trained virtually?

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Yeah, for Bill Intro 406.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Well, the training can be virtually.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: So for co-ops and for boards, you have does both in-person on-site trainings at the building.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: So you have to do both or you can choose one?

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: They do both, and they also do online, like so teletrainings, and then they also hold trainings in their own offices, which multiple buildings can attend simultaneously.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: And I do also have concerns similar to Councilmember Mercedes-Narcisse District.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: We have...

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: My district is not a wealthy, wealthy district.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Our property tax is higher than Park Slo.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: And the Park Slo parents send their kids to my district schools.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: We are paying, our neighborhood is paying other neighborhoods property tax.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: So we really...

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Hope you guys can look into it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Yes, we are currently working on property tax reform.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Yeah, because you have wealthy neighborhood paying less, less wealthy neighborhood paying more.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: It's not fair to people living in New York City.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: And the next question for...

chapters.summary: Zhuang asks if the city can direct co-op boards to resources to lessen expenses, noting maintenance charges have increased 20-25%. Carrión discusses HPD's preservation pipeline, subsidized funding, and the need for modest annual maintenance increases.
chapters.title: Zhuang asks about resources for co-op boards facing rising costs

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Will, because give the district contact between city stakeholders and the co-op board members, that is a unique opportunity for conversation.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Co-op board members are currently struggling to adhere to many local laws that impact co-ops due to the rising costs.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: They require.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: These costs are being passed to stakeholders, many of those who are in fixed income.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: In some cases, stakeholder maintenance charges have been increased 20 to 25 percent over the last few years.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Can we use this point of connecting to direct a co-op board member to resources available to them to lessen these expenses?

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: So this is a part of the plan?

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: Yeah, so I should say two things about this.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: One is we do have, through our normal preservation work at HPD, the ability to work with co-ops who are in need of capital improvements.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: When we do that, and we do about 1,200 units a year,

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: through our preservation pipeline of limited equity co-ops.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: This is subsidized funding, so that helps us not have to raise or have the co-op raise maintenance significantly.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: That said, I do think the other thing we're struggling with when we're working with both our Michilama and our HDFC co-ops is that there are many years where they don't impose any rent increase, in some cases 10, 12, 30 years,

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: and then they start to not be able to maintain their debt or their monthly expenses.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: So we are always working with our cooperators to educate shareholders about the need to impose modest rent increases

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: on an annual or maintenance increases on an annual basis so that they don't find themselves suddenly having to do a 20% or an 18% increase in a single year.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Do you have translation support for those trainings?

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: They do.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Okay, thank you.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Thank you, Councilmember Zhuang.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: We'll now go to Councilmember Brewer, followed by Thomas Henry.

chapters.summary: Councilmember Gale Brewer asks how many buildings remain in TIL, how many opted out of HDFC, vacancies, restrictive deeds, and about two specific buildings. Carrión provides some data (60 buildings left to convert, ~250 regulated HDFCs) and will follow up on the addresses.
chapters.title: Brewer asks HPD for HDFC data and updates on specific buildings

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Thank you for the update on the land bank.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I had it, but it's nice to see it in writing.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Number two, just in terms of data, and if you did this already, I apologize, but how many of the HCFCs are still in till that you...

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Proposed to convert to HDFC, that's question number one.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: How many have opted out of HDFC?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: They always have to pay a property tax, but they don't like being in it and they want to go make a lot of money.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: That irritates me.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Number three, just to...

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: How many vacancies are in HCFCs, if you know?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: People, unfortunately, do have vacancies.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: How many have no restrictive decks is another question.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I know quite a few of them don't, and they are playing fast and furious.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I also got a call the other day, and I should have been able to answer it, but at what point...

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Does the HCFC, as I call it, I know there's a new term for it, property tax kick in, if at all?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: And finally, 59 West 87th Street, a lot of drama in terms of...

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: persons assigned to work with the residents, residents don't get along.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: So I'd like some help with that building.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: And finally, 615 West 150th Street, I put in millions of dollars as BP.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I want to know what the update is.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: Thank you, Council Member.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: So there's a lot.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: I'll try to take them all.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: On the question of how many buildings remain in ANCP or TIL, basically, there are 60 buildings left to convert.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: Again, we did about four conversions last year or started construction on four last year, and we've done four this year, and we expect to do a few more before we get to the end of the fiscal year.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: On the vacancies across all HDFCs, I don't think we know.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: As I said, we regulate only about 250 of the existing, say, 1,300 or so or 1,400 HDFCs.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: So we would only be able to report vacancies on the ones that we actually regulate.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: And I don't know that we know the question on the restrictive decks.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: If you're talking about regulatory agreements, again, it's about 250 that we regulate.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Out of the 1,400.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: About out of the 1,400.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: And others may get the damp tax cap.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: So they do have restrictions, but they're not directly regulated by HPD.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: And then on the two buildings, I think I'll need to follow up with you post this because I don't.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: Are these both HDFCs?

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: They are.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I know every HDFC in Manhattan.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: And both of these are existing HDFCs that need wine?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: 59 West 87th Street is.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: One is not, I don't believe.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Palente.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: Uh-huh.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Controls 615 West 150th Street.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: And I want to know what's the status of that building.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: In fact, generally, Palente, are you working with them to convert?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Because that's why you're going slowly.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: So as you probably know, there's a team at HPD that is working with all of the buildings that remain until all 60, as well as those that are actually now through construction and getting ready to convert.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: And we have had a long history with Puente working with them.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I was part of it.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: So I don't have an answer for you today, Councilmember, but I wrote down the two addresses.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: We'll happily get you updates.

chapters.summary: Brewer says technical assistance may not be enough and asks if HPD has an extensive board strategy for HDFCs. Carrión says the $7 million UHAB contract works with all HDFCs, including those not regulated by HPD.
chapters.title: Brewer questions HPD on board strategy for HDFCs

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Okay, and then just finally on the boards, I know you're getting technical assistance, et cetera, but that's not necessarily going to work.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: You really need an extensive board.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: strategy.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Are you really thinking you're going to have one with this new technical assistance?

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: That's for the Mitchell Llamas.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: No, but I'm talking about for HCFC.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: So you have no technical assistance for HCFC's boards?

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: There is.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: So the $7 million contract that we have with UHAB is really dedicated to working very deeply with specific boards as well as all.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: And that includes yours that you're overseeing or their balance of the 1400?

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: They do work with all of ours and those that we recommend to them as needed, or sometimes they go directly to UHAB because that's what they're known for, but they will also work with any of the 1400 HDFCs.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I'll leave it at that, but you have a big problem there.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: Okay, so now we're going to call on Thomas Henry.

chapters.summary: Councilmember Shanel Thomas-Henry asks how property taxes on co-ops are assessed, noting her co-op's taxes doubled. Shear explains state law requires valuing co-ops as rental properties, and offers to look into her specific case.
chapters.title: Thomas-Henry asks DOF about co-op property tax assessment methodology

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Hello, thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: My first question, I know property taxes are a hot topic, but can you explain currently how the property taxes on co-ops is assessed?

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: Can you give a little more detail?

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: So, okay, so the property taxes, and I'm just going to say my co-op in particular, has more than doubled over the past few years.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: And when I asked the representative from finance at a community meeting, they said the methodology or the calculation is based on the current market rental value of said unit.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: So really I want to see is that accurate or?

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: So currently state law requires us in valuing co-ops and condos to do so as if they were rental producing property.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: So we need to find a comparable building and look at its...

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: Income per square foot and use that to come up with the assessment and market value of the co-op.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: There can be other factors.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: So that's been the law for many years.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: So that wouldn't necessarily impact the value.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: There can be expiring exemptions that can also impact the taxes.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: So if you would share with me the details, we're happy to dig into it and provide you with some more information.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: So I think the issue, and not just my building, but a lot of buildings in my district, these are owners who have been there for generations.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: And while the...

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: And there are no, what's the word I'm looking for, subletting.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: So essentially, these homeowners are paying for a value that they can't benefit from.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: So those units aren't being rented at market rate.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: They're essentially homes that their parents passed down to them or whatever.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: So they're not profiting off them.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: However, many people who are on a fixed income are now paying property taxes at a rate that they can't afford based on a methodology that doesn't seem fair in that circumstance.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: But I know that's a hot topic and more to get into with the state.

chapters.summary: Thomas-Henry asks about the success rate of the $4 million in funding for foreclosure prevention attorneys. HPD says 830 clients were served, 200 had successful resolutions, and the process takes time. She asks about a list of bad actor lenders.
chapters.title: Thomas-Henry asks about foreclosure prevention success rates

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: The $4 million in funding for attorneys for foreclosure prevention, do we have any insight in terms of how many modifications or foreclosure prevention are successfully?

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: We do, and I'm going to have my colleague come up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Yeah, so last year of the, I think it's 830-something clients that were served with intensive one-on-one counseling.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: with our partners across the city, 200 last year had a successful resolution.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Do we know why the 600 plus were not successful?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So this is a process that takes time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So you're working with what we consider a successful resolution would be, you know, they have a mortgage modification.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: They're sort of like they're done with the process.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: They've successfully saved their home.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: They have a mortgage modification.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: They have changes to their.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: They've gone through financial counseling.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: They're sort of on sure footing with their home.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: They paid off their unpaid debt.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So these things take time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: They might be entering into a payment plan.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: It might take time to figure out what the right payment plan is or to go back and forth with the bank to achieve that modification.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So within any given year, you're not going to solve every single homeowner's problems, and things might carry over.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: No, understood.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Do you have a list similar to how you keep like a bad landlord list, like a list of lenders who have not been good actors and negotiated in good faith to make sure that our homeowners stay in their homes?

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: I don't have a current list.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: I'm reflecting back to my time at the Attorney General's office, which during the foreclosure crisis, I think it was pretty well known which banks had been.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: Committing abuses.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: I do think that has gotten better since the foreclosure crisis, but I will be frank, there are some lenders who do not operate in good faith.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: We are very lucky in New York State to have a consumer protection set of laws that give homeowners that are in foreclosure the right to

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: go before a judge.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: and negotiate directly with the bank through a system called the settlement conference process.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: So it is not untrue that some lenders continue to try to evade the requirements that certainly came out and the improvements made after the foreclosure crisis, but we are also lucky to have this huge network.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: Of legal service providers and housing counselors who stand by tenants and, I'm sorry, homeowners and represent them in that process.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: And if we find, if a homeowner finds that there is a bad actor, who do they contact to let know?

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: The homeowner helped us.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Thank you, Councilmember Thomas Henry.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Back to Chair Lee.

chapters.summary: Lee clarifies that Intro 1084 is meant to prevent lien sale, and asks about DOF's payment plans, defaults, and website clarity. DOF lists six payment plans, reports 3,144 Class 1 owners removed via plans, no foreclosures last year, and provides default numbers.
chapters.title: Lee follows up on Intro 1084, payment plan defaults, and website clarity

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: Okay, great.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: Sorry, so just to clarify and give extra context, because I had a conversation with the bill sponsor, Crystal Hudson, on 1084.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: And this bill really is meant to prevent folks from going into the lien sale process.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: So I just wanted to put that out there.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: And there were some questions that she had wanted me to ask.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: So in terms of 1084, what processes does DOF currently have in place to assist taxpayers with property tax payment shortcomings for the identified homeowner populations covering the bill?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Well, we do have six different payment plans right now that we offer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Yep.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: We have the standard payment plan.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: We have the reduced rate.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: We have a low-income senior PT8 plan.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: We have the fixed income base PT8 plan.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: We also have extended circumstances income-based PT8 plan as well as the circuit breaker payment plan.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So there are six different opportunities that we offer to assist homeowners to go into a payment plan.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And once you're in the payment plan, you are removed from the lien sale.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: Okay, so...

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: And I would just add as well that...

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: We do a lot of notices and outreach sessions where we feature the availability of payment plans.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: We do it on our property tax bills that go out quarterly to most homeowners.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: We do it on our annual notices of property value.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: And we do our delinquency notices, which I talked a lot about earlier.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: We always contain information about exemptions and payment plans.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: We also do outreach sessions.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: So we do outreach sessions.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: Every January and

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: February associated with the notices of property value and we do a lot of outreach during the tax lien sale outreach process

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: to make sure that homeowners that are in the at-risk pool are aware of the payment plan options.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: Okay and how many languages do you send out the notifications in?

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: We have translations available for, so I don't know if we send them out in other languages, but

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: I do know that when we send out our bills, we notify people of the availability that we have in all the languages that are required by local law.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: Okay, in the language, right?

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: So they can read it?

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: I'm just checking.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: No, because I know that when I was working in the nonprofit side in the community for many years, that was one of the frustrations that we had with a lot of the notifications coming from the city is that they were not in language.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: And so a lot of folks would get these notices and not understand or have any idea of what that was.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: And I just ask that because I wonder if that also can contribute to some of the folks that may not be enrolled that are eligible.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: Okay, and then enrolling in a payment plan removes a property from the tax lien sale list.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: So how many payment plans defaulted in 2025 by plan type, if you have that breakdown?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: I don't have those numbers right now, but we'll be happy to get that to you.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: And how many Class 1 owners were removed from the list by enrolling in a plan?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: For the last lien sale, we had 3,144 Class 1 owners enrolled in the payment plan and were removed from the list.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: That were removed?

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: Okay, and gone.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: And how many homeowners lost their homes through tax lien foreclosures in the past year?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: We had none.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: None, okay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: We had no foreclosures in the past year.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: That's good.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: And what staff and resources do you have currently reviewing applications for payment plans under the current system?

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: We'll have to get back to you on that.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: Okay, and do you believe, if a follow-up to that question is, do you believe the current staff you have could handle the workload of the new opt-out system proposed with this legislation?

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: I mean, I know that you said no, yes, and then your testimony, but just for the record.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: Yes, for the record, no, we would need more staffing.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: We don't have an estimate today.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: And obviously, how much staffing we need would depend on the ultimate scope of the bill.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: As we've discussed, depending on the target population, the larger it is, the more staffing we might need to support it.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: And DOF's website presents the standard payment plan, the PTA payment plans, and the reduced interest payment plans.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: three separate options.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: However, PT8 enrollees automatically get the reduced interest, and those in the standard plan are also eligible but need to apply for both the standard plan and lower interest, but the website's messaging makes it sound like you cannot do both.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: When was the last time DOF reviewed the website for clarity, and have you had outside review to ensure that this info is clearly presented?

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: So in preparation for this hearing, we had people review the website, and they want to politely disagree.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: They think that it is clear, but we're happy to sit down with you or your staff member to see if there's something that we are overlooking.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: Okay, thank you.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: And, you know, just as a note, we do look forward to having more conversations and fleshing out the bill because I think the goal and the intent, as you said, is a good one.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: So hopefully we can continue working on that with you.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: So thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Chair, I do have the default numbers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: I didn't realize.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Oh, sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: For the between.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: February of 2025 to the end of July, for the standard payment plan, $4,141 defaulted.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And for the reduced rate, 33 defaulted.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And for PT8, 101 defaulted.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: Sorry, what was the second number?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: The reduced rate to 33.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: Okay, thanks, Chair.

chapters.summary: Sanchez asks about HPD's position on DAMP renewal and engagement with the state. Carrión says urgent need to renew, positive conversations. She also asks about lien sale outreach contracts; Carrión says HPD has a $2 million contract with the Center for NYC Neighborhoods for outreach.
chapters.title: Sanchez asks about DAMP renewal and lien sale outreach contracts

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair Lee.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: So my second round, and we're going to continue with other council members.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: So starting off with DAMP, the majority leader's resolution calls on the state to pass the HDFC Fairness, Preservation, and Affordability Act, sponsored by State Senator Robert Jackson and Assemblymember Al Taylor.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: With the DAMP tax cap,

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Set to expire in 2029, does HPD have a position on how the state and the city can work together to create a long-term preservation plan from limited equity co-ops?

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Have you engaged with the state on this issue?

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: And if so, how have those conversations gone?

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: So we agree there is a fairly urgent need to renew the damn tax cap.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: It obviously creates a limiting factor for co-ops if they need to refinance with uncertainty about the future of the tax abatement.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: We have had several conversations with the bill sponsors at the state, our partners in the state legislature.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: I would say they were very positive conversations.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: I think we made some recommendations about some of the rules that we would like to see included in the renewal of the damp tax cap, mostly about maintaining affordability and then also maintaining, as I was discussing earlier,

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: a modest maintenance increase on an annual basis where needed in order to ensure that they don't get in future financial difficulties.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Appreciate getting that on the record.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: I also want to follow up on Councilmember Silvina Brooks-Powers'lines of questioning around the lean sale, actually pivoting to DOF, lean sale outreach.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: You know, previous council under Speaker Adams dedicated or negotiated some funding for outreach,

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: specifically want to ask about engagement with outside organizations, CBOs that have the on-the-ground knowledge to reach

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: the communities, the homes in the communities that are most at risk, like Councilmember Brooks-Powers, like Councilmember Banks'districts.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Can you tell us, I know you said you don't have the dollar amount today, so we'll wait on that, but can you tell us about how your conversations are going with external CBOs to conduct that outreach?

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: Yeah, so I will, just because Michael Schaap holds the contract for the outreach specifically to make sure we're getting to folks who may be on the lien sale and also were on past lien sales.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: So it is a $2 million contract for one year.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: The Center for New York City Neighborhoods is our primary sub-recipient, and they are in the process of onboarding, they think, between 15 and 20 sub-organizations who are more community-based and locally-based.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: A lot of that will be based on the advanced notification that DOF provides to them so that they know exactly where, by address, where the homes are.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: that are going to be impacted by the upcoming lien sale.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: The center is committed to a very deep dive for everybody who is going to be included in future lien sales, including eight touch points with each homeowner.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: That will include things like mailings, texting, phone calls, door knocking, and then in-person counseling.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: Including community meetings.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: So we are very glad that the center has sort of already launched and is ready to go well in advance of any future lien sale and feel that there will be very, very aggressive outreach to make sure every homeowner knows what the options are.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: And just to supplement that with the outreach that we do as a government agency, in addition to the great work that HPD does with the not-for-profits,

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: we have a robust outreach effort when it comes to the tax lien sale outreach period.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: And we are committed to doing two sessions in each of the 10 council districts that have the most properties in the outrush pool.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: That's exactly the question she wanted answered, so thank you so much for highlighting that.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Excellent.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Sanchez asks about the Office of Deed Theft Prevention's progress, staffing, and goals. DOF says the office has 3 staff and an ombudsman, has received 300 complaints since March, and is working with advocacy groups and law enforcement.
chapters.title: Sanchez asks DOF about Office of Deed Theft Prevention progress

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: So then my next question is, and we started to talk a little bit about the Office of Deed Theft Prevention, but I'm hoping for an update in

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: connection with its stated goals, right, to educate homeowners, to conduct public outreach, to review suspicious property.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: filing, support investigations and enforcement efforts to help homeowners report suspected deed theft, promote tools that alert homeowners to changes in property records and to help victims navigate the property record correction.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: This office was created in March of this year.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Can you tell us how many staff are dedicated to the Office of Deed Theft and how you are progressing in these goals of this office?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: We have three staff members dedicated to the office.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: We also have an ombudsman that also works with the office in reviewing the claims that come through.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Just repeat the second part of your question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: So just in connection to the goals of the office, what progress is DOF making?

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: And specifically, you know, I think it's really important that the agency is able to develop a way to alert property owners of suspect, well, of odd or suspicious property filings.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: And helping homeowners through the process.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: So where are you in the process?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: The office has been meeting with elected officials.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: They work with advocacy groups, law enforcement officials to establish strong working relationships and exchange ideas and strategies for how we can best combine different cooperation efforts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: I don't have the exact list of where the director has, but we'll be able to share you the different groups we have actually reached out to and where we are with all of that, working with the strategies.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: I would just also add to that.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: There are many agencies.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: And offices that work on the deed theft problem.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: It's a huge problem.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: It spans many different areas.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: And simply having a single point of entry for concerned citizens, we think has been a tremendous step forward.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: And as a result of that, the office has received

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: 300 deed theft complaints since its inception.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Since its inception in March.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Wow.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Got it.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Sanchez asks how DOB protects homeowners adjacent to construction sites, referencing a recent tragedy. DOB says they send notifications to adjacent owners, have site safety triggers, and starting next year will require one dedicated construction superintendent per site.
chapters.title: Sanchez asks DOB about notifications to adjacent property owners

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Okay, so I had another question in connection, and this is for the Department of Buildings, in connection to something that Councilmember Joseph raised earlier, and that is how the Department of Buildings protects

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: homeowners who are living adjacent construction sites, which of course is on everyone's mind following the horrific tragedy last week at 1321.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: So I'm going to save that question except for Deputy Commissioner if you want to

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: comment on how the department works with or alerts or requires alerts for adjacent

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: and property owners when there's going to be a construction project next to their property.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Thank you, Council Member.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So when a construction project is proposed next to someone's property, we do send out notifications to those property owners, letting them know what construction work is going to occur next door to them, who the contractor is, what the permit number is,

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: insurance information related to the contractor as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And there are site safety triggers depending on the type of work that's going to be conducted.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: For example, new building work, demolition, a large alteration that will require a construction superintendent, for example.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Beginning next year, we're going to be implementing a local law that the council passed a few years ago that ramps down the number of sites that a construction super can be responsible for.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Previously, it was 10.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Starting next year, it will be one, so there will be a dedicated construction super at all of these construction sites.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And we can certainly pull together a more thorough list of site safety supervision triggers that are.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Apply to these construction sites as well.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Got it.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Thank you, Deputy Commissioner.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: And just foreshadowing so that you all are ready on during Friday's hearing that we really want to talk about the department's work at smaller sites, right?

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: So the smaller buildings, those that are less than 75 feet tall, seven stories, understanding that that's an important threshold for the agency.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: We want to understand how you're keeping New Yorkers safe on those sites and in those buildings.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Understood.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Thank you, Deputy Commissioner.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: So now on to round two, I want to call on Deputy Speaker Williams, followed by Councilmember Joseph.

chapters.summary: Deputy Speaker Williams asks about Intro 1096 and expresses frustration with the lack of progress on property tax reform, asking if there are state sponsors. Shear says they do not yet have a bill and it's premature to discuss sponsors.
chapters.title: Williams presses HPD on Intro 1096 and DOF on property tax reform

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: I didn't see any comments on 1096.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Did I miss it?

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: You didn't miss it.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: I addressed it in my opening, but I'm happy to answer any questions about it now.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: I read the opening.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: I didn't see it.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Yeah, if you can, because I didn't, I mean, I read the opening myself.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: I didn't see 1096 anywhere.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: I think the spirit of the bill is something we support, and I think we would like to have a conversation probably to go a little deeper with your office on what, because I can quickly reiterate.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: The services that are already provided through the homeowner help desk are fairly expansive and very targeted.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: So I think we would like to understand better what you think is missing from that array of services and whether additional legislation is necessary to accomplish that.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Okay, thanks.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: On the property taxes, the mayor said this in January, and it's November.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: And so I just want to...

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Albany is like going to be back up and running in like short order.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: So I just want to understand a little bit more about the bill, the strategy.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Do you have state sponsors to carry the bill?

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Just wanted to understand like what is actually happening and if it's really going to happen and not just saying it's going to happen because that's what you all have been.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: saying for a very long time.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: We do not yet have a bill.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: We are working on developing a bill.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: And because we do not have a bill, it's premature for us to be talking about sponsors and so forth.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: I mean, I will say that I know the state has repeatedly said that they're waiting for the city to send something up.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: And so I think if you are working on something as a matter of like intergovernmental

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: state strategy, that there should be conversations with the leadership or potential bill sponsors, because what is what good is it to have legislation if you don't have people who actually push it forward in the state?

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Like it's not like the council, like it's a different body.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: So.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: That said, I have concerns.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: I do not believe that you all really care, and I do not believe you all are actually actively working towards property tax reform.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: So that's just like my personal opinion.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: There's been no updates.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: The mayor's office, DOF, has said nothing to me since he said, since they all said they were going to do something when you all made the proposal to raise property taxes.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: I know that was a whole big debacle at the beginning of the year.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: And a part of that was the mayor committing to figure out how the city could play a role and set something up around property tax reform.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: But I literally, outside of like questions that have come before this hearing, I have not heard a single thing that DOF has done or City Hall has done.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: And then to just say you're going to have.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: this bill, I mean, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: I think if you've ever, I'm sure you're more experienced than me, if you've ever done any advocacy with Albany, like, you really have to start early.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: So I'm just, do not believe that you guys are, like, going to do anything or get anything done this legislative session.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: I would be shocked, and I look forward to being shocked, and I look forward to being wrong.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: If I could just do the whole...

chapters.summary: Williams asks for data on Southeast Queens homeowners contacting the help desk, referrals, and outcomes. She also asks if agencies can link DOB, DOF, and HPD data, and requests deed theft clinics and senior exemption help in her district.
chapters.title: Williams requests data on help desk outcomes and interagency data sharing

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Cheat code with asking a whole bunch of other questions um and then hopefully you can answer them

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: so just measuring results um with hpd i would love to know how many southeast queens so between me brooks powers and hangerson's district

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: um homeowners contacted the help desk last fiscal year how many completed referrals what outcomes were available to verify and what happens when the referral stalls for dob and finance

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: following a case just really wanting to understand how your agencies interact so can you link dob records with finance lien data and hpd foreclosure data to see whether the same properties appear at later stages can you

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: distinguish when a dob related charge was part of a lien from cases where a property had other unpaid charges um

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: back to deed theft local access would love if a team could join southeast queens to do some clinics to help homeowners sign up for deed theft alerts and refer suspected fraud for prompt review

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: um and same thing with assistance so if you could share with us where our office can contact about urgent cases that would be helpful um

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
