utterances.text: For finance, same thing, like really looking for further engagement for many of the seniors living in my district, making sure that they know about the exemptions.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: So not sure if you'll have the capacity to actually provide on-site application help at the senior centers in my district.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: And then for HPD, I don't know if it's HPD or DOF, if you provide assistance maybe through the homeowner advocate's office for folks who are looking to clear titles.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: So when homes are inherited and deeds are still in a deceased relative's name, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: I don't think my office has clear understanding of, like, tax relief or any type of assistance that can be provided in the meantime.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: And then I know Senator Comrie shared we're planning to send a letter

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: to DOB because there's some issues with cost of correcting violations for owners of one and two family homes who cannot afford required repairs and when expectors

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: tell them about financial technical help, who should be follow up on those referrals.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: So natural gas alarm guidance, help with the alarm costs for your reduced cost alarms would be helpful.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: And then lastly, I promise I'm done to DOB on my other bill.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: I know you don't track race and socioeconomic status, but New York City is a pretty stratified city by race.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: And so just also want to understand, like, if you track, I know you.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: you know where you've gone as DOB to certain areas in New York City.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: And so if you can actually share that data, that would be helpful because I think it'll still tell a story about where we're generating revenue from.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: And if we are equitably generating revenue across New York City, or are we only targeting certain communities, which again, we're a stratified city.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: So if you talk geography, we know where the black folks are.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: We know where the Latinos are.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: We know where the white folks are.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: It's like we know where they are across the city.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: And so even if you're not collecting data on race,

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: it would be helpful to have an understanding, you know, by zip code of where these violations are occurring.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: So anyone can start.

chapters.summary: Carrión responds to Williams' questions, mentioning the $1 million estate planning and resolution contract with the Center for NYC Neighborhoods, and a new diagnostic tool for tangled title. He asks for data requests in writing.
chapters.title: Carrión responds on tangled title resources and data requests

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: It's a little, there's a lot there.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: I would ask on the Southeast Queens questions, which is the first one that you raised, we do have a lot of that information from the homeowner help desk.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: So if you could send us sort of all the questions or send me directly.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: If I need to follow up, I will.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: But yeah, we're just trying to understand and get more clear data.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: And then, so yes, if you send us a request with all the data points you're looking for, any of those that we have, obviously, we would be happy to share with your office for whichever of the districts you're interested in.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: You did raise a question about tangled title and what are homeowners to do when they have issues with, right, really complex title transactions.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: There is this new outreach on estate planning and resolution contract that we have also with the Center for New York City Neighborhoods through the Homeowner Help Desk.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: It's a million dollars per year, and it is direct outreach to address those exact types of issues.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: There was a forum happening actually simultaneously with this hearing today at the Furman Center where they're trying to develop a new diagnostic tool to sort of predict where tangled title is happening so that we can be more targeted in the outreach.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: But there is new resources available run also through the Homeowner Help Desk specifically to help folks with that.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: And if folks don't really know how to access that, please reach out.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Make sure your district knows.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: You're the deputy speaker?

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: We looked at...

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: We look forward to following up with you, Council Member.

chapters.summary: Sanchez co-signs Williams' emphasis on the need to progress with property tax reform conversations this year, noting the council has been discussing it for years.
chapters.title: Sanchez co-signs urgency for property tax reform

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: I just want to co-sign the emphasis on the need to make sure we actually progress with the property tax reform conversations this year.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Because, yeah, I mean, we've been talking about this as council members for five years, but even before that, no, I'm going to call you Jeff, but, you know, WD Commissioner, I share that we've been talking about this.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: I don't even, I don't want to date us.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: I don't want to date you.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: So now we're going to turn it to Councilmember Joseph, followed by Amelie, then Wong.

chapters.summary: Joseph asks for a timeline on property tax reform and for deed theft data for Brooklyn Community Boards 14 and 17. Shear says they are working on a bill for the upcoming session, no specifics, and will get back on the data.
chapters.title: Joseph asks DOF for timeline on property tax reform and deed theft data

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Earlier we talked about the property tax disparities, and you said you have no timeline.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Is there, you didn't even give a timeline.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Is there a timeline on working on that?

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Just co-signing with my colleague here, because this is something we hear across the district in these flatbush that I represent.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: We are working on a bill for the upcoming state legislative session.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: Beyond that, I do not have more specifics.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: See now, see, Councilman, Deputy Chancellor.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Deep TEF complaints have tripled between 2020.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: How many of this year's complaint came from Brooklyn Community Board 14 and 17?

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: And how many of these homeowners actually got their deed back?

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Is there data as to who received their deed back?

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Y'all look puzzled.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: No one never gets their deed?

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: One person got their deed back?

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: We will get back to you, Council Member, on both questions.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: So you will share that data with my district office?

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: Yes, we will.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Okay.

chapters.summary: Joseph asks about lien sale outreach, including door-knocking and partnering with clergy. Carrión describes the $2 million contract with 15-20 sub-organizations and 8 touch points per homeowner. Joseph also asks how many seniors lost exemptions due to paperwork; Shear will get the number.
chapters.title: Joseph asks about door-knocking outreach and seniors losing exemptions

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Lean sales, when we talked about earlier, in terms of reaching out, is there actively to knock on doors, outreach?

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Are we partnering with clergy?

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Are we setting up meetings in communities?

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Are you going where the people are?

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Are you reaching the folks on the ground, my older adult who may not?

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Have their papers anymore.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Talk to me about that.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: Yes, Council Member, I'm going to answer that because, again, this is under the contract that HPD holds with the Center for New York City Neighborhoods.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: It's a $2 million contract.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: As I said, they are going to be bringing on somewhere between 15 and 20 sub-organizations who are more community-based, and because DOF will make advance...

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: We'll provide advanced information to the center on exactly who we expect to see on the lean list before the 90-day list comes out publicly.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: The center and their subs will have the opportunity to go deep into the neighborhoods at an address-specific level to start the outreach process.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: Because I also said they've agreed to do under our contract eight touch points with every homeowner.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: Some of that will be in person.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: Some of that will be texts.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: Some of that will be phone calls and emails.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: And some of it will be like...

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: Tabling at events at DOF.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: And you know our older adults are targeted for scams, so they may not trust you as well.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: We understand, which is why we think it's very important that the center work with local community-based organizations who might be more recognizable to seniors and to other populations within these communities.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: So we will be doing a ton of outreach in advance of the lean cell list coming out.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: SCHE and DHE helped about 53,000 households.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: How many seniors lost the exemption last year because of missed renewal or paperwork or not because they were actually ineligible?

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Do you have a number?

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: I don't have a number with me.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: We will get that to you, Councilmember.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: A lot of getting back to me.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: And I will follow up so you will get back to me.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Because that data will drive a lot of our policy, a lot of our budget.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: It's sad to see our communities of color lose their homes because of a simple mishap.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: So we look forward to working with you.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: And I co-sign with all of my colleagues on the record on following up and making sure we're holding these agencies accountable.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Thank you, Councilmember Joseph.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Councilmember Mealy, followed by Thomas Henry.

chapters.summary: Mealy returns to the issue of homeowners charged for relocation expenses after vacate orders, citing $2,000/month charges for nearly two years. Carrión explains ERP liens and the emergency housing process, and says he will follow up with her office.
chapters.title: Mealy follows up on ERP liens and relocation expense charges

utterances.speaker: Darlene Mealy
utterances.text: Yes, I just have a follow-up.

utterances.speaker: Darlene Mealy
utterances.text: You never answered the question.

utterances.speaker: Darlene Mealy
utterances.text: Did you know, do you have a department for that?

utterances.speaker: Darlene Mealy
utterances.text: Like if relocation expenses, call HPD.

utterances.speaker: Darlene Mealy
utterances.text: HPD don't know.

utterances.speaker: Darlene Mealy
utterances.text: Department of Finance, they don't know.

utterances.speaker: Darlene Mealy
utterances.text: Then we got a number.

utterances.speaker: Darlene Mealy
utterances.text: It said call 212-863-6020.

utterances.speaker: Darlene Mealy
utterances.text: Call them.

utterances.speaker: Darlene Mealy
utterances.text: They said, no, you have to just email.

utterances.speaker: Darlene Mealy
utterances.text: And that's gutierrez at hpd.nyc.gov.

utterances.speaker: Darlene Mealy
utterances.text: So people are getting all these tickets, well, all these prices that they, on their property tax, from their house, from HPD, on their property tax.

utterances.speaker: Darlene Mealy
utterances.text: So then they said a relocation expenses at hpd.nyc.gov.

utterances.speaker: Darlene Mealy
utterances.text: Who is doing these?

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: So I think we're talking about two different things, but help me if I'm mistaken.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: But it's still dealing with...

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: The ERP liens that HPD does file when we get a complaint from a tenant who is living in, say, an owner-occupied two-family home, we under law have to go out and inspect.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: We get a complaint.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: If we have to spend money to force the repair or to make the repair ourselves, that does become an ERP lien, and those liens then are converted to DOF, where they may become part of a tax bill.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: In the last lien sale...

utterances.speaker: Darlene Mealy
utterances.text: Is it a law on that?

utterances.speaker: Darlene Mealy
utterances.text: Because I checked.

utterances.speaker: Darlene Mealy
utterances.text: I had lawyers check.

utterances.speaker: Darlene Mealy
utterances.text: It's nothing stating that HPD...

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: Uh-huh.

utterances.speaker: Darlene Mealy
utterances.text: Can put a bill on your property tax.

utterances.speaker: Darlene Mealy
utterances.text: So how can that...

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: ERP liens under local statute, not just for homeowners who have rentals, but for all buildings, do get transferred eventually if unpaid to DOF.

utterances.speaker: Darlene Mealy
utterances.text: So if it's not unpaid, this was a tenant, if you evict someone, no.

utterances.speaker: Darlene Mealy
utterances.text: If you vacate order.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Darlene Mealy
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Darlene Mealy
utterances.text: So now if the vacate order, what do you do?

utterances.speaker: Darlene Mealy
utterances.text: You put them in a hotel.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: So if there is a need to vacate, and typically that's for whatever reason, whether it's fire or something else.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: And you charge them?

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: No, we have a service through our Office of Code Enforcement, something called Emergency Housing Shelter.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: We have a contract with the American Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: The Red Cross will then come out and serve anybody who needs temporary housing in a hotel.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: It's automatic that they will get between two and four days of temporary shelter for folks who then need longer-term shelter if we can't get folks returned back home.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: The HPD oversees, I think it's three family shelters and seven SRO shelters where we provide longer-term housing for anybody who needs it for the duration that they're out of their home.

utterances.speaker: Darlene Mealy
utterances.text: So this is not a hotel.

utterances.speaker: Darlene Mealy
utterances.text: It's a combination of both.

utterances.speaker: Darlene Mealy
utterances.text: You've been keeping them in a...

utterances.speaker: Darlene Mealy
utterances.text: All right, you keep them in a hotel.

utterances.speaker: Darlene Mealy
utterances.text: For how long?

utterances.speaker: Darlene Mealy
utterances.text: You could keep them for a year and then charge the homeowner $2,000 a month on their property taxes.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: So the hotel stay does not usually exceed two to four days.

utterances.speaker: Darlene Mealy
utterances.text: So something is wrong.

utterances.speaker: Darlene Mealy
utterances.text: We have to talk because I have numerous of people where $2,000 a month for almost two years.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: Yes, Councilmember.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: And then it goes to their property tax.

utterances.speaker: Darlene Mealy
utterances.text: That is something wrong.

utterances.speaker: Darlene Mealy
utterances.text: And then not to have a department or a person.

utterances.speaker: Darlene Mealy
utterances.text: that you could speak to to try to rectify it, something is wrong.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: Well, we do have a department through E&S, through our Office of Code Enforcement, and I'm happy to follow up with your office and get any information.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: For anybody who's been charged, again, that doesn't match.

utterances.speaker: Darlene Mealy
utterances.text: I asked to speak on this body, and she couldn't tell.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: Well, I will certainly follow up with your office.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: I could also add that HPD has a general line, so if folks are having trouble reaching HPD, they can always contact us at 212-863-6300 and speak to an HPD navigator who will help them kind of navigate around and find the

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: right team at the HPD to talk to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: It's a very large agency.

utterances.speaker: Darlene Mealy
utterances.text: You know we did all of that.

utterances.speaker: Darlene Mealy
utterances.text: And $3 million is a lot of money.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: That is a lot of money.

utterances.speaker: Darlene Mealy
utterances.text: For someone, six-story building, not a multi-dwelling development.

utterances.speaker: Darlene Mealy
utterances.text: That's the small business and homeowner that we are just crushing.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Again, a reminder that audience participation, I love it, but is not allowed.

utterances.speaker: Darlene Mealy
utterances.text: They need the number, though.

utterances.speaker: Darlene Mealy
utterances.text: Let's flood them.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: And if you have any questions for our illustrious panel or my colleagues, please pull them to the side as they walk out.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Thank you, Councilmember Mealy.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Now I'd like to turn it to Councilmember Thomas Henry, followed by Wong.

chapters.summary: Thomas-Henry asks how incentives for affordable rental vs. homeownership development compare. Carrión says term sheets are comparable. She also asks about interest rates on late property taxes; Shear says rates vary and interest is not forgiven if paid in full.
chapters.title: Thomas-Henry asks about developer incentives and property tax interest

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Okay, a couple of quick questions.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: As we talk about more opportunities for home ownership,

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: How would you compare incentives for developers building affordable rental units versus building home ownership units?

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: So our term sheets are pretty comparable between homeownership development and rental development.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: There's usually a set developer fee that's named explicitly in our term sheets.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: And it's not more or less advantageous to do homeownership development than it is to do rental, except that at the end of the process, you don't own the building.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: So some developers are only interested in being long-term owners.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: They're obviously not the sponsors we work with to create affordable homeownership opportunities.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: We get overwhelmingly a number of those who aren't looking for home ownership opportunities.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Have you had, but they're the same developers over and over again.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Have you had conversations with them about moving towards home ownership?

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Versus rentals?

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: We have actually seen more development partners interested in sponsoring affordable homeownership.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: We're now working with a couple of actual for-profit groups who have partnered with us through the ANCP process to sponsor the conversion, right?

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: Because in that program, we do require that there be a developer.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: Partner to the tenants during the process.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: So I don't think we've struggled much, at least in my time in the agency, to have a deep bench of affordable housing producers who want to sponsor co-ops.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: But if there are organizations out there that are interested, that you're aware of, that are curious about how our term sheets work, we do take meetings like that all the time where folks are interested in how, generally there's some confusion about how limited equity co-ops work at all.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: But if they were interested in being sponsors, we would love to have more sponsors, though I would not describe it as a shortage.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Next question is for finance, and I have a question for business, if you, Department of Buildings, if you want to switch over.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Currently, there are no penalties if your property taxes are late, correct?

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Or just interest?

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: Just interest.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: And what are those interest rates?

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: They vary based upon the...

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: The value of the property and whether you're in one of our payment plans.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: I don't have the rates off the top of my head.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: But we will get you all of the rates that we charge.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: At any point in time, if the property tax are paid in full, is that interest forgiven?

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: No, it is not.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Okay.

chapters.summary: Thomas-Henry describes homeowners fined for basement apartments that were not being rented. DOB describes the Homeowner Relief Program, extended cure periods, and a review of the penalty schedule for small property owners.
chapters.title: Thomas-Henry asks DOB about fines for basement apartments

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: DOB, as the deputy speaker mentioned, there are a lot of fees that are being assessed on a lot of single family and two family homeowners from your department.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: In particular, I found in my district that I've had a couple of people find where they have homes where, say,

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: one of their children or someone is living in a basement and you guys have fined them for it being not being up to code as if it was a rental.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: And I can attest to some of these basements that have never been rented or used as such.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: So how do you assess and work with the homeowners in situations like that?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Specifically for small property owners, we've launched a couple of programs in recent years to allow them opportunities to correct before they receive any penalties.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: For example, the Homeowner Relief Program is specific for one- and two-family homeowners.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: That will give them 60 days to correct violating conditions without incurring any traditional violation or monetary penalty.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Also, in late 2022, we extended the cure periods for all of our Class 2 and Class 3 violations across the board from 40 to 60 days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So that provides even more opportunity to correct before incurring any monetary penalties.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And something that we're looking at currently is the penalties that we impose to small property owners.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So we're undertaking a review of our penalty schedule to determine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: and whether there's any right-sizing of the penalties that we need to do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: But as it relates to the specific situation that you're describing, happy to follow up with you and get more details.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Councilmember Thomas Henry.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Now I'd like to turn to Councilmember Wong.

chapters.summary: Wong asks if the city has a single point of contact for homeowners and if agencies share data on at-risk homeowners. Carrión says the Homeowner Help Desk is the single point of contact, with $10 million in funding, and agencies share data with the Center for NYC Neighborhoods.
chapters.title: Wong asks about single point of contact and interagency data sharing

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: For homeowners that are in distress, they often have to keep track of a lot of their debts, lock into the Department of Buildings, and then Department of Finance, and then the HPD, and so forth.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: My question is,

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: They obviously need help.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: It's not just they don't have, especially those with language barriers, it can be a very demanding task to keep track of the depths.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: My question is, does the city have a single point of contact for homeowners?

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: And my follow-up to that is, do the three agencies share data on homeowners that are at risk of losing their homes?

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Please answer them.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: We do.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: So I would say the best single point of contact is what we've talked about a lot here today, which is the homeowner help desk, which was created specifically to be

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: whether you're looking for help avoiding foreclosure, whether you have liens that you have to settle with the city, or whether you have tangled title, all of the services start with the homeowner help desk.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: That is now a combined total of $10 million that we are funding for a series of programs that I've covered a lot about.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: today.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: So that is the best single point of contact.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: So that will list all the debts?

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: Well, no, it doesn't list all the debts.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: It is where you would get connected to a counselor who could help you understand exactly what your challenges are or what you need to know.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: As it relates to your question about information sharing, all the agencies, and certainly HPD and DOF, are funneling information into the Center for New York City Neighborhoods as the predominant operator of the homeowner help desk.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: And then lastly, I would say, and we talked about it also, we publish a very robust handbook called the Homeowner Handbook every year in nine languages that gives folks a very specific

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: directive on who to call depending on what issue they're struggling with.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Okay, one follow-up.

chapters.summary: Wong asks how much of the governor's $40 million Homeowner Protection Program goes to NYC. Carrión says $14 million goes to 30 organizations in NYC, and HPD does not receive any of it directly.
chapters.title: Wong asks about state Homeowner Protection Program funding

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: The governor pledged $40 million in the state fiscal budget for the homeowners protection program.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: And how much of that is going to New York City?

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: $14 million comes to 30 organizations in New York City out of the governor's protection program.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: And how much is your agency getting?

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: We don't get anything.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: It goes directly to the providers.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: So this is a contract that it's actually run through the Attorney General's office, and each of the 30 providers have a direct contract with the AG.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: But collectively, those 30 organizations are getting $14 million out of the $40 million allocated annually.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Great, thank you, Councilmember Wong.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Member Chair Lee.

chapters.summary: Lee asks if payment plan notices will show amounts due and who to call to switch plans, and suggests joint outreach with DOF, HPD, and DEP in Eastern Queens. DOF will get back on the notice details; HPD and DOF agree to joint outreach.
chapters.title: Lee asks about payment plan notices and joint outreach with DEP

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: Sorry, just had a couple follow-up questions.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: More district-specific, because as you know, my district is all the way in eastern Queens.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: I have northeast Queens and southeast Queens, and most of my district are homeowners.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: And I actually have the largest number of co-ops and condos in my district, which people wouldn't think, but we actually do have the most number of units.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: And just really quickly, if the lowest cost plan, mostly to DOF, if the lowest cost plan has payments they can't afford, will the notice also show what's due each time and who they can call in their language to switch plans, right?

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: So if they're enrolled in a plan, they want to switch, and it's not really meeting their needs, is it going to show how much is due each time and who they can call if they need to switch?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: I will get back to you on that, Council Member.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: And then lastly, because a lot of the homeowner issues are usually together,

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: would DOF and HPD, would you think and consider working with DEP to offer regular walk-in hours in Eastern Queens so homeowners can get help with property taxes and water bills in one visit?

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: Because a lot of times there's issues with both.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: And my district is a transit desert, and we have a lot of older adults, and so would love to see if we could have more outreach in the actual community.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: I don't want to speak for DOF, but I would argue we would be delighted to do a joint outreach session and include DEP as well as our partners at the homeowner help desk.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: We also would be delighted.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: Okay, perfect.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: I'm going to hold you guys to that.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair Lee.

chapters.summary: Sanchez asks when the council can expect a red line on Intro 657, the Safer Homes Act, which was promised by mid-November. Carrión apologizes for the delay, affirms support, and promises to follow up with the law department, hoping before Thanksgiving.
chapters.title: Sanchez asks for red line on Safer Homes Act (Intro 657)

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: And I have one final question, which Commissioner Levy, you will know, is completely on brand.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: But I have to put this out there.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: So speaking of converting rentals to homeownership opportunities and speaking of reforms intended to improve tax collections, but also improving conditions for New Yorkers and protecting and promoting homeownership,

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: this committee has heard the reform of the third-party transfer bill three times since I have been chair of the Housing Committee and as recently as March of this year.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: As chair, I'm intent on reforming the tool into an absolutely new program, as you know, because principled municipal foreclosure through the third-party transfer route

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: is one of the city's most consequential tools for, or can be the most, one of the city's most consequential tools for addressing distressed properties.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: The administration has had the council's red line since you began, since the mayor took office, and while we have had several discussions on the substance of the legislation, red lines have been stalled.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: In September, the administration committed to me personally and to the council to continue in conversation with the red line in mid-November, which I define as November 15th.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: It is November 17th.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: And so my question, Commissioner, and this is to both.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: DOF and HPD is when, when, when, when can we at the council expect to receive a red line on Intro 657, the Safer Homes Act, and is this still a priority for the administration?

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: So, yes, I am sorry that it has taken so long.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: It is a complicated bill, but I can say that we affirmatively support the bill.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: We've been actually talking about it quite a bit with the committee that's forming, sorry, the board members that are now forming the land bank and how.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: Our expectation that the Safer Homes Act will come back and how that will work with the land bank has been very much on our minds.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: I can't remember if you can attest to that as a board member.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: Got a witness on her side.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: But I will personally follow up with our friends at the law department to find out, you know,

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: If we're two days late, you know, can we try to get you a copy of this, hopefully before Thanksgiving, before we break next week?

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: It is not an indication of any lack of support for the bill.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: I think it's just complex and everybody is doing a lot of stuff.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: But that is not an excuse, and I will personally find out where we are.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Thank you, Commissioner.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Thank you to my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair Lee, for hosting this hearing together with us.

chapters.summary: Sanchez thanks her colleagues and Chair Lee, and concludes the agency portion of the hearing. She asks if someone from the agencies can stay to hear public testimony, and then moves to the public comment period.
chapters.title: Sanchez closes agency testimony, moves to public comment

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: With that, your portion has concluded, and we're going to move to the public's testimony.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: And if the agencies could have someone stay behind to hear the public, we would really appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: All right.

chapters.summary: Sanchez reminds the public that this is a formal proceeding, asks for decorum, and explains that speakers will have two minutes, must fill out appearance cards, and can submit written testimony within 72 hours. She then calls the first panel.
chapters.title: Sanchez outlines rules for public testimony

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: I'm going to move us along here to the public comment period.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: So I will now open the hearing for public testimony.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: I remind members of the public that this is a formal government proceeding and that decorum shall be observed at all times.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: As such, members of the public shall remain silent at all times.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: The witness table is reserved for people who wish to testify.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: No video recording or photography is allowed from the witness table.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Further, members of the public may not present audio or video recordings as testimony, but may submit transcripts of such recordings to the Sergeant at Arms for inclusion in the hearing record.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: If you wish to speak at today's hearing, please fill out an appearance card and with the Sergeant at Arms.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Excuse me, an appearance card with the sergeant at arms and wait to be recognized.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: When recognized, you will have two minutes to speak on today's hearing topic of advancing homeownership and protection.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: including introductions numbers 406, 861, 862, 1082, 1084, 1091, 1096, 1097, and resolutions number 9, 147, 363, and 599.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: If you have a written statement or additional written testimony you wish to submit for the record, please provide a copy of that testimony to the Sergeant at Arms.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: You may also email written testimony at testimony at council.nyc.gov within 72 hours of this hearing.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Audio and video recordings will not be accepted.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Also, if you email it to me, which people very often do, I will probably lose it.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: So make sure you use that testimony at council email.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: And with that, we're going to call the first panel.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: And I just want to state, I mentioned this at the top of the hearing, I'm dealing with a personal matter, so I'm going to co-chair with Chair Lee the rest of the hearing remotely.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: And so please don't take that as an affront.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: I am listening.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: I just, you know, sandwich generation, you have to care for those who cared for you.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Okay, so the first panel up is going to be Kevin Wolf, Asita McGee, apologies if I mispronounce that, Marianne Rothman, and Ms.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Rachel Ciprian.

chapters.summary: Kevin Wolf, Director of Policy and Research at the Center for New York Homeownership, commends the council for over $7 million in resources for housing counseling and legal services. He supports the bills and suggests integrating Home First with first-time homebuyer education and the Housing Connect portal.
chapters.title: Kevin Wolf testifies on council's historic investment in homeowner protection

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kevin Wolf
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kevin Wolf
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kevin Wolf
utterances.text: I will make this short.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kevin Wolf
utterances.text: Thank you for the opportunity, Chair Sanchez and Chair Lee, to testify today.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kevin Wolf
utterances.text: My name is Kevin Wolf.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kevin Wolf
utterances.text: I am the Director of Policy and Research at the Center for New York Homeownership.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kevin Wolf
utterances.text: We recently changed our name.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kevin Wolf
utterances.text: And first, I want to just commend the council for stepping up to the plate and making a historic investment to protect New York homeowners.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kevin Wolf
utterances.text: The council committed to over $7 million in resources for housing counseling and legal services, including $2 million for tax lien-specific outreach.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kevin Wolf
utterances.text: This will ensure that the homeowners that are under threat for foreclosure, tax liens, deed theft, and eviction will have access to lawyers, housing counseling, and financial counselors free of charge.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kevin Wolf
utterances.text: While homeowners advocates across the country are facing funding cuts, delays, and erosions of their rights from the Trump administration, New York is leading the nation.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kevin Wolf
utterances.text: Our 1.1 million homeowners have significantly more

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kevin Wolf
utterances.text: protections and resources thanks to the council that are critical to preserving their homes.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kevin Wolf
utterances.text: For the bills that have been considered today, collectively we believe that they represent an important step in the right direction.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kevin Wolf
utterances.text: We want to recognize the proposal from Deputy Speaker Nantasha Williams on anti-displacement.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kevin Wolf
utterances.text: We have a district profile service.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kevin Wolf
utterances.text: And we'd be happy to work with her on providing data for homeowners at risk of displacement.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kevin Wolf
utterances.text: In addition, I'm getting a little bit of an echo, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kevin Wolf
utterances.text: In addition, Councilmember Brooks Powers for the intro, age 61,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kevin Wolf
utterances.text: we would encourage the council to examine the best practices across the nation and just do a study on what's worked and try to streamline the federal rules and also work with the congressional delegation to advocate for more federal resources.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kevin Wolf
utterances.text: On the intro 861 for Home First, this is very important.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kevin Wolf
utterances.text: We would just like to see it integrated with first-time homebuyer education and the Housing Connect portal.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kevin Wolf
utterances.text: Finally, if I could just one last sentence, on behalf of the homeowners who do the work and who

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kevin Wolf
utterances.text: play by the rules, on behalf of the hardworking New Yorkers who are struggling to afford to live in this city, we want to repeat our view that no homeowner should lose their home because of the tax lien.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kevin Wolf
utterances.text: If the tax lien sale must move forward, homeowners must have meaningful protection and access to legal services and housing counseling with every opportunity to pay their debt and remain in their home.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Adolfo Carrión Jr.
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Asita McGee, a Southeast Queens resident, describes being targeted by a predatory scout and the fear it caused. She supports the bills and asks the council to add Intro 879 for responsible home sharing to provide supplemental income for homeowners.
chapters.title: Asita McGee shares personal experience with predatory deed theft

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Asita McGee
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Asita McGee
utterances.text: My name is Asita McGee.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Asita McGee
utterances.text: I live in Southeast Queens, District 27.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Asita McGee
utterances.text: Predatory D-theft is real.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Asita McGee
utterances.text: And I have an experience.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Asita McGee
utterances.text: A neighbor overheard a conversation with a new neighbor.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Asita McGee
utterances.text: Inquiring of which neighbor lived in the community the longest.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Asita McGee
utterances.text: I was named, then targeted.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Asita McGee
utterances.text: I was asked if my mortgage was paid.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Asita McGee
utterances.text: My daughter was asked how much income my property generates.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Asita McGee
utterances.text: Because I worked in the private and public sectors as a financial analyst, I knew what this meant.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Asita McGee
utterances.text: I have advocated for my community since owning my home from 1986.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Asita McGee
utterances.text: I felt drained.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Asita McGee
utterances.text: The blood just went out.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Asita McGee
utterances.text: I don't even know how I got back into my house.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Asita McGee
utterances.text: The person was a predatory scout, and there were people assigned to do the deed theft.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Asita McGee
utterances.text: So predatory D-theft is real.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Asita McGee
utterances.text: Financial vulnerability is real for seniors and people in financial transition.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Asita McGee
utterances.text: And I've been here.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Asita McGee
utterances.text: I'm hearing that you all are addressing things, and I just love what I'm hearing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Asita McGee
utterances.text: I'm going to walk out of here with way more confidence than I had before.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Asita McGee
utterances.text: Responsible home sharing is a way to help us stay independent in our homes.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Asita McGee
utterances.text: The set of bills on the agenda is amazing, and we are so glad the council is discussing homeowners and affordability.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Asita McGee
utterances.text: We need your help with supplemental income and would encourage you to add Intro 879 to the set of bills on the agenda today.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Asita McGee
utterances.text: Once again, my name is Asida McGee, District 27, Dr.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Asita McGee
utterances.text: Natasha Williams District, and all of Southeast Queens.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Asita McGee
utterances.text: We have a high foreclosure rate, so certainly we need supplemental income.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Asita McGee
utterances.text: I would encourage you to add Intro 879 to the set of bills on the agenda.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Asita McGee
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Mary Ann Rothman, Executive Director of the Council of New York Cooperatives and Condominiums, says CNYC already provides extensive education for co-op boards. She supports Intro 406's outreach mandate and offers to work with HPD to reach more boards.
chapters.title: Mary Ann Rothman supports Intro 406 on co-op board training

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mary Ann Rothman
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mary Ann Rothman
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Chair Sanchez and Lee and member of the committee.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mary Ann Rothman
utterances.text: My name is Mary Ann Rothman.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mary Ann Rothman
utterances.text: I'm the Executive Director of the Council of New York Cooperatives and Condominiums,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mary Ann Rothman
utterances.text: a membership organization that's been providing information, education, and advocacy for more than 50 years to a growing membership of economically and geographically diverse,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mary Ann Rothman
utterances.text: resident-owned, owner-governed co-ops and condos.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mary Ann Rothman
utterances.text: In any given year, CNYC presents scores of classes, workshops, and discussions to help board members and potential board members learn their responsibilities,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mary Ann Rothman
utterances.text: implement best practices, and remain current with changes in the law.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mary Ann Rothman
utterances.text: CNYC is submitting detailed written testimony on many of the items under discussion today.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mary Ann Rothman
utterances.text: I'll limit my time to comments in support of Intro 406 that seeks to establish a board member training program and requires city outreach to make boards

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mary Ann Rothman
utterances.text: aware of the education available to them.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mary Ann Rothman
utterances.text: I would argue that the educational programs prescribed in Intro 406 already exist.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mary Ann Rothman
utterances.text: My organization has long been educating co-op board members in fiduciary responsibility.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mary Ann Rothman
utterances.text: responsibilities, best practices, financial management, long-term capital planning, governance, compliance, risk management, capital project management, admissions,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mary Ann Rothman
utterances.text: reasonable accommodations, employer responsibilities, discrimination law, the Fair Housing Act, community building, and more.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mary Ann Rothman
utterances.text: Our speakers are experts in their field with years of successful co-op and condo experience to share.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mary Ann Rothman
utterances.text: But we haven't been able to reach all of the cooperative boards who could benefit from more education.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mary Ann Rothman
utterances.text: CNYC has classes, materials, experience, cooperative knowledge, and technical knowledge to help HPD deliver cooperative education to boards.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mary Ann Rothman
utterances.text: The outreach mandated by Intro 406 should bring more boards to the table.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mary Ann Rothman
utterances.text: We look forward to working with the council and with HPD on this important endeavor.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mary Ann Rothman
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Sanchez announces that the council is planning a hearing in January or February on threats to affordable housing cooperatives, including rising operating costs, insurance, Local Law 97, and access to city supports. She welcomes feedback.
chapters.title: Sanchez announces upcoming hearing on threats to affordable co-ops

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: I just wanted to mention while I have you, this is, I think this is relevant to everyone, but especially Marianne, because we've been having so many conversations about the sustainability of affordable co-ops, condos.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: What if I sing?

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Should I sing it?

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Would that make it less uncomfortable?

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: But we are planning in the council, we're planning a hearing in maybe January, maybe end of January, early February on the threats to affordable housing cooperatives and all of this,

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: specifically with respect to the rising costs of operating these structures.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: So, you know, compliance with city laws, for instance, which you've raised in other conversations, access to city supports from tax incentives, but all the way to things like one-shot deals for co-ops that

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: have shareholders that have fallen behind, and then insurance, insurance, and then again insurance.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: So I just want to put that on your radar and welcome your feedback in advance of the conversation, but also during the conversation at the hearing.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: And compliance with local law 97.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: I was going to say, can we add local law 97 to that?

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Thank you to this panel.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: Okay, great.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: So I'm going to call up the next panel.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: We have Bradley McCormick, Christopher Fasano, Matthew Dunbar, and Ariel Hirsch.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: And feel free to begin when you're ready.

chapters.summary: Ariel Hirsch, Director of Policy at UHAB, supports Resolution 9 but suggests tweaks for affordability, enforcement, and equity. She notes UHAB's training contract covers about 1,200 HDFC co-ops and asks for clarification on training populations.
chapters.title: Ariel Hirsch testifies on DAMP tax cap and HDFC preservation

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ariel Hirsch
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ariel Hirsch
utterances.text: Fun stuff with the mic today.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ariel Hirsch
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Chairs Lee and Sanchez and member of the committee.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ariel Hirsch
utterances.text: Thank you so much for the time to testify and for holding this hearing, especially focusing on homeownership.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ariel Hirsch
utterances.text: My name is Ariel Hirsch, and I am the Director of Policy at UHAB.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ariel Hirsch
utterances.text: For 50 years, UHAB has empowered low- and moderate-income residents to take control of their housing and supported communities by creating strong and lasting affordable cooperatives, specifically HDFC and Mitchell Lama cooperatives.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ariel Hirsch
utterances.text: We will submit longer written testimony, but I want to focus, since there's so much going on at our hearing today, on a few key points.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ariel Hirsch
utterances.text: The first is on the damp tax cap.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ariel Hirsch
utterances.text: We are so appreciative of Majority Leader Abreu for bringing this issue into the council conversation and for the engagement of Chair Sanchez, Councilmember Riley, Salam, many others with high proportions of HDFCs in their district.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ariel Hirsch
utterances.text: This is, of course, an urgent issue for HDFC cooperatives, and we think it's really important to get right

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ariel Hirsch
utterances.text: the preservation mechanism for this essential stock of about 25,000 units of affordable homeownership for current and future generations of New Yorkers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ariel Hirsch
utterances.text: We think that the state bill that's included in the intro here needs a

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ariel Hirsch
utterances.text: a few more tweaks to be just right for the full stock.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ariel Hirsch
utterances.text: And along some three pillars, the first is affordability, including that HDFCs remain affordable for current and future residents through this tax reduction and

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ariel Hirsch
utterances.text: ensure that affordable sales prices keep these buildings affordable for future generations of New Yorkers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ariel Hirsch
utterances.text: We think that there's also an enforcement piece here.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ariel Hirsch
utterances.text: The legislation needs a slightly clearer enforcement structure that includes some basic information to ensure that if an HDFC is out of good standing, there is a recourse and there's an option here.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ariel Hirsch
utterances.text: And we also are really interested in partnering with the agency to build capacity and asset management and oversight, which we think there's just not enough support for at the moment.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ariel Hirsch
utterances.text: The third issue here is equity.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ariel Hirsch
utterances.text: The existing damp tax cap has been distributed inequitably across the city where homeowners, especially in the Bronx, have received much less tax benefit than others across the city.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ariel Hirsch
utterances.text: This needs to be redistributed in our current program and accounted for retroactively for those buildings that have not gotten the same level of support.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ariel Hirsch
utterances.text: May I conclude very briefly?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ariel Hirsch
utterances.text: I also want to include briefly on my testimony, we spoke a lot about training.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ariel Hirsch
utterances.text: UHAB holds the current HMMT and technical assistance and training contract to support HDFC cooperatives, but that is only for about 1,200 HDFC co-ops.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ariel Hirsch
utterances.text: throughout the city.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ariel Hirsch
utterances.text: It does not include, there we mentioned a Mitchell Lama RFP that's going out at the moment,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ariel Hirsch
utterances.text: but it does not include market rate co-ops, which Marianne spoke about in her testimony, and just would love to see the bill clarified around training about which specific populations and how those fit with the existing infrastructure that we have for training, which

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ariel Hirsch
utterances.text: we need more support always to really reach the number of folks who need this to run and maintain their buildings.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ariel Hirsch
utterances.text: Thank you so much for your time.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: I would like to get credit for taking you with me.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair Sanchez, and no one doubts your dedication to this issue and many others.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Bradley McCormick, attorney at Brooklyn Legal Services, corrects the record on 2026 tax lien foreclosures, opposes the 2027 lien sale, and supports the POWER Act with a private right of action. He suggests narrowing the small business exemption to cover deed theft perpetrators.
chapters.title: Bradley McCormick testifies on deed theft, tax lien sale, and POWER Act

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bradley McCormick
utterances.text: Thank you very much for holding this important meeting on homeownership protection.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bradley McCormick
utterances.text: My name is Bradley McCormick.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bradley McCormick
utterances.text: I'm an attorney for the Homeowner Rights Unit at the Neighborhood Economic Justice Project at Brooklyn Legal Services.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bradley McCormick
utterances.text: I represent homeowners who have been victims of DITA.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bradley McCormick
utterances.text: And I'll add that before I joined Brooklyn Legal Services, I worked at the Department of Consumer and Worker Protection for 13 years.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bradley McCormick
utterances.text: Before I begin my prepared comments, I may have misheard something in the city's testimony, and I just want to make sure that the committee is clear that there have been tax lien foreclosure

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bradley McCormick
utterances.text: auctions in 2026, including a homeowner who owed $20,000 in tax arrears on a property DOF

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bradley McCormick
utterances.text: valued at $1.5 million that was sold at foreclosure auction for $1 million.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bradley McCormick
utterances.text: New York City's at-risk homeowners, especially those in communities of color who are disproportionately targeted for home equity stripping scams, would be helped tremendously by the POWER Act and by halting the 2027 tax lien sale.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bradley McCormick
utterances.text: The Department of Finance will soon publish the 2027 tax lien sale list.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bradley McCormick
utterances.text: This operates as a lead generator for scammers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bradley McCormick
utterances.text: I recently deposed one of the city's most prolific deed theft and partition scammers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bradley McCormick
utterances.text: He admitted that he specifically seeked

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bradley McCormick
utterances.text: out properties with tax liens for so-called investment.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bradley McCormick
utterances.text: The tax lien sale, whereby the city sells delinquent tax liens to Wall Street investors, makes the city's complicit in deed theft crisis plaguing the most vulnerable homeowners.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bradley McCormick
utterances.text: The Power Act, which would ban unfair business practices,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bradley McCormick
utterances.text: would be an effective, lasting tool to protect New York City homeowners and consumers more generally.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bradley McCormick
utterances.text: The Power Act gives DCWP an important tool that's been missing from its toolbox.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bradley McCormick
utterances.text: However, DCWP's resources and authority are finite, so a private right of action is an important supplement to enforcement.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bradley McCormick
utterances.text: By DCWP.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bradley McCormick
utterances.text: There is, however, one provision of the proposed Power Act that could make it less effective as a protection for homeowners.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bradley McCormick
utterances.text: The bill exempts small businesses from the Power Act's private right of action.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bradley McCormick
utterances.text: However, perpetrators of deed theft are likely to fall into this exception.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bradley McCormick
utterances.text: Real estate fraudsters typically form business entities for the sole purpose of purchasing a specific one-to-four family home.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bradley McCormick
utterances.text: They own two or three properties at most.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bradley McCormick
utterances.text: They rarely have any employees, and they don't gross $5 million in annual revenue.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bradley McCormick
utterances.text: This bill would be far more effective in addressing deed fraud and other scams with a less expansive carve-out for small businesses.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bradley McCormick
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mary Ann Rothman
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Christopher Fasano, Supervising Attorney at the Legal Aid Society, supports Intro 1096 but argues the POWER Act (Intro 1105) is needed to curb deed theft. He describes the high evidentiary burden for victims and urges the city to abandon the 2027 lien sale.
chapters.title: Christopher Fasano supports Intro 1096 and POWER Act

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Christopher Fasano
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Chair Lee and Councilmember Mealy.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Christopher Fasano
utterances.text: My name is Christopher Fasano.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Christopher Fasano
utterances.text: I'm the Supervising Attorney of the Foreclosure Prevention Project at the Legal Aid Society.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Christopher Fasano
utterances.text: The Legal Aid Society supports Intro 1096, which would direct outreach to communities most affected by threats to homeownership.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Christopher Fasano
utterances.text: But while Intro 1096 would improve access to services, the Council can do more to preserve homeownership by passing the Power Act, which is Intro 1105.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Christopher Fasano
utterances.text: Currently, New York is one of only seven states that permits companies to engage in unfair, deceptive, and abusive business practices without facing accountability from the people whom they've harmed.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Christopher Fasano
utterances.text: The Power Act would bring New York City in line with the vast majority of jurisdictions that already enable residents to seek redress for these financial wrongs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Christopher Fasano
utterances.text: For homeowners, the Power Act would curb one of the most pernicious financial scams plaguing the city, d-theft.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Christopher Fasano
utterances.text: Under existing law, victims have to prove fraud to hold these scammers to account, which is a very high bar.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Christopher Fasano
utterances.text: This evidentiary burden is often insurmountable because scammers are usually sophisticated enough not to reduce any of their lines to writing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Christopher Fasano
utterances.text: Worse yet, the very vulnerabilities that scammers target, things like age-related memory loss, also make it harder for homeowners to prove their case.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Christopher Fasano
utterances.text: The Power Act would flip that paradigm.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Christopher Fasano
utterances.text: Targeting a senior itself would be an abusive business practice.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Christopher Fasano
utterances.text: In short, while an outreach event can help connect homeowners to legal services, if that homeowner lacks

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Christopher Fasano
utterances.text: acts basic legal rights, that outreach accomplishes much less than the homeowner rightfully expects.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Christopher Fasano
utterances.text: In addition to passing the Power Act, the city can refrain from certain actions that jeopardize homeownership.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Christopher Fasano
utterances.text: Just last week, the city announced a whole tax lien sale, which we talked about quite a bit this morning.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Christopher Fasano
utterances.text: I do want to emphasize that apart from the negligible benefit, fiscal benefit the city realizes, and the obvious harm it causes homeowners, the harm extends beyond the homeowners whose liens are sold.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Christopher Fasano
utterances.text: And that's because it reinforces the structural racism embedded in New York City's housing market, as 72% of the liens sold for one to three family homes in 2025 were in majority Black and or Hispanic neighborhoods.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Christopher Fasano
utterances.text: Resuming the tax lien sale during escalating affordability crisis undercuts the council's efforts in this package of bills to preserve homeownership and stabilize neighborhoods.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Christopher Fasano
utterances.text: It also undermines the mayor's agenda to make the city more affordable for working class New Yorkers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Christopher Fasano
utterances.text: We urge the city to abandon this ill-conceived policy.

chapters.summary: Matt Dunbar, Chief of Staff at Habitat for Humanity NYC and Westchester, supports streamlining the senior and disability exemption, renewing the DAMP tax cap, and expanding voucher homeownership. He notes NYCHA does not currently participate in the voucher homeownership program.
chapters.title: Matt Dunbar testifies on senior exemption, DAMP, and voucher homeownership

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matt Dunbar
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matt Dunbar
utterances.text: My name is Matt Dunbar.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matt Dunbar
utterances.text: I'm the Chief of Staff with Habitat for Humanity in New York City and Westchester County.
